title: Preface
text: Preface An account of AI centric software development Puma wants this book to explain the thinking behind a great deal of practical work with software agents, and to expose that thinking to criticism. These are complementary aims. A method becomes easier to criticize when its assumptions and consequences are visible. It becomes more useful when readers can decide which parts fit their own work. The subject is a way of connecting purpose, design, implementation, and evidence. AI agents make that connection unusually important. They can produce plausible code quickly, distribute work across multiple tasks, and maintain extensive records. They can also elaborate an assumption that nobody meant to make. A coherent plan, a clean architecture diagram, or a passing test suite can preserve a misunderstanding rather than expose it. Practical engineering work provides the setting for the examples. Recurring questions concern resource lifecycles, execution, coordination, knowledge representation, and provenance. The examples make decisions, assumptions, and consequences inspectable; readers need not reproduce a particular collection of projects to examine the reasoning. The case studies do not establish a finished, proven method. Nor do they show that every declared practice is followed consistently. A published standard says what its consumers should do. Source code shows a particular implementation. A test observes behavior under its conditions. A conversation explains an intention. These are different kinds of evidence, and the differences matter. The account uses third-person references to Puma where describing stated views or inspected work. The explanations, exercises, and proposed alternatives are the book's synthesis. They should not be mistaken for quotations, a transcript of Puma's development sessions, or a claim that every suggested technique is already in routine use. How to use this book The chapters follow a change from an uncertain request to a usable result, then ask what happens when many such changes become an ecosystem. You can read them in order or start with a current problem. A developer struggling with resource ownership may begin with chapters 7 and 25. Someone coordinating several agents may start with chapters 18 through 22. A reader evaluating the approach critically may find chapters 27 and 31 useful companions to the opening. A running example keeps the discussion concrete: an application acquires a local resource so another component can use it. Sometimes that resource is a model. The illustrative system has enough moving parts to expose identity, readiness, cancellation, ownership, and acceptance, but it is illustrative rather than a reconstruction of any one implementation. Each example states the behavior under discussion instead of expecting familiarity with that repository. The exercises ask you to make decisions and produce inspectable artifacts. They do not require adopting a particular agent product or reproducing Puma's technology stack. You can perform most with a small application and an ordinary version-control workflow. The work should remain proportional. If an exercise exposes no consequential uncertainty in your task, record that conclusion and use the simpler path. Experienced practitioners appear where they illuminate an actual choice. Their accounts include enthusiasm, restraint, failures, and changes of mind. Academic and technical sources provide additional distinctions and counterweights. Neither testimony nor a benchmark validates this entire method. References are included so you can inspect the basis of a claim rather than accept it on authority. The repository cases are pinned to revisions inspected on 2 October 2026. Local tests were not rerun for this book; where results come from project reports or hosted logs, the wording says so. Living external sources were checked during the same research period. Software and model capabilities will change. The durable questions concern ownership, feedback, evidence, and the cost of decisions, not a permanent ranking of products. The strongest criticism will identify a specific claim, an omitted condition, or a credible alternative. Perhaps a proposed boundary creates more work than it removes. Perhaps a record is too expensive to maintain. Perhaps an ordinary implementation followed by a demonstration would discover the problem faster. Those are useful objections. The book succeeds if it makes them easier to formulate and investigate.

title: 1 Start with the outcome
text: Part 1 Finding the system worth building Begin with the result someone needs, then develop enough shared understanding to choose the next step. Investigation and prototypes remain part of that understanding; the aim is a defensible commitment rather than a complete prediction of the future. 1 Start with the outcome An agent is asked to make a downloaded model available to an application. It adds a download operation, writes bytes to disk, returns success, and tests that the file exists. The application still cannot use the model. Perhaps the model needs a companion file. Perhaps a runtime is missing. Perhaps the local catalog does not know its identity. Perhaps success was announced before finalization finished. These are different defects, but the request left one question unresolved: what does available mean? This is an illustrative scenario. Its purpose is to show how an implementation can satisfy a literal interpretation while missing the intended result. Puma has described this problem directly: a plan may be logically consistent and still omit an invariant that would have changed what the agent built. Nothing inside the plan necessarily contradicts the omission. Executing the plan more faithfully cannot recover information that never entered it. An outcome states what becomes possible for someone. An implementation describes how the system makes it possible. The distinction is useful without being absolute. A mechanism can itself be a requirement when compatibility, regulation, interoperability, or a deliberate product choice makes it essential. The developer needs to discover why a requested detail matters before treating it as either binding or disposable. Find the action after success For the download example, ask what the consumer should do immediately after receiving success. If the answer is “open the selected version through the supported runtime,” file existence is only an intermediate condition. The system must also make the selection resolvable and establish whatever readiness the runtime requires. A first outcome statement could be: After the operation succeeds, the intended local consumer can request the selected resource by its stable identity and begin using it through a supported runtime. The statement still needs discussion. Does the acquisition operation install the runtime? Does it report missing support? Can it substitute another model? Those choices affect the product and should not be hidden inside an attractive method name. Now add an unwanted result: The interface says the operation succeeded, but the consumer receives an artifact it cannot identify or use. This counterexample gives the team something concrete to exclude. It does not select an architecture. It establishes that “download returned success” is an inadequate acceptance observation for the intended outcome. The same method works outside model management. If a request says “add export,” ask what the recipient must be able to do with the exported data. If it says “make search faster,” ask which delay is disrupting which activity. If it says “use a graph,” ask what relationships the person needs to see or which decision the graph should support. Separate purpose from a plausible representation Suppose a person wants a graph of a codebase. They may be trying to understand dependencies, locate the reason behind a decision, assess the impact of a change, or identify unfinished work. A graph of file imports may help with the first and fail at the others. A useful question is, “What would you want to notice or decide more quickly?” It respects the suggestion while investigating its purpose. The person might explain that spatial relationships are essential to how they work. In that case, a visual requirement is real. Or they might reveal that they mainly need a reliable answer to “Why is this here?” A graph could remain useful, but the data now needs to include reasoning and provenance rather than merely structural links. Do not convert this into a ritual in which every request is challenged. If the outcome is clear, the requested mechanism fits, and the change is bounded, proceed. Discovery has a cost. Its value lies in resolving a decision that affects the result. Keep the domain assumptions visible Software operates in a world it does not completely control. A program can verify a checksum, but it relies on an expected checksum with a trustworthy origin. It can publish a local path, but it relies on filesystem behavior and permissions. It can ask a process to stop, but the request is not the same event as confirmed termination. Requirements research distinguishes desired world outcomes, software specifications, and assumptions about the environment. Zave and Jackson's formal account makes the relationship explicit: the software's specified behavior and domain assumptions must together support the required outcome. This is a conceptual foundation, not proof that a particular conversation finds every assumption. Four Dark Corners of Requirements Engineering . For our resource example, an assumption might be that publishing a reference can be made atomic with respect to readers. If that assumption is false on a supported platform, a correct implementation of the planned sequence may still expose a partial result. Naming the assumption lets someone investigate it before the plan treats it as settled. Try it on a small change Choose a request you could implement in a day. Write five short statements: The person or component that needs the change The action it should be able to perform afterward One superficially successful result that would disappoint it One environmental assumption needed for success One detail whose status as a requirement or preference is unclear Explain the result back to the requester. Include a consequence they did not explicitly mention. If your export includes private metadata, your faster search returns stale results, or your download silently installs a runtime, that consequence belongs in the discussion. The artifact should be short enough to remain useful during implementation. It is a reference point, not a promise that no further learning will occur. When the code changes, it gives the team a way to ask whether the new behavior still serves the original purpose.

title: 2 Discover intent through conversation
text: 2 Discover intent through conversation A good discovery conversation changes what the participants understand. It does not merely collect answers for headings in a plan. Puma's concern is that consequential details often remain unstated because they seem obvious, have not yet occurred to the requester, or only become visible when a proposed solution is examined. An agent can fill those spaces with reasonable assumptions. The resulting design may look complete precisely because its assumptions are internally consistent. The conversation should therefore expose choices that matter, while leaving room for both the person and the agent to revise the picture. Ask questions that can change a decision Consider the resource acquisition example. Asking “What programming language should we use?” may be premature if the work belongs in an existing component. Asking “What should the consumer see while the new version is being checked?” may reveal a product invariant. The second question can change the design. The person might require the old version to remain usable, accept a temporary unavailable state, or want both versions addressable. Those answers imply different identity and publication behavior. A useful question has a plausible connection to a decision; it is not simply something the agent could ask. Questions also need sequence. Begin with concrete situations the person understands. Ask how they use the current system, what goes wrong, and what they expect next. Introduce technical alternatives once the distinction they represent is clear. Otherwise the person may choose an option based on a name while misunderstanding its consequences. Avoid leading formulations. “Wouldn't a reusable service be better?” invites agreement with an unexplained conclusion. “Two applications need this behavior; should they share one process, or is independent operation important?” identifies a real tradeoff. Even that question may need an example before the person can answer. Keep different kinds of statement separate The discussion may contain an intention, an observation, a constraint, a preference, a hypothesis, and a decision. They do not need six files, but they should not collapse into one undifferentiated list. “The model must work offline” could be a firm requirement. “The existing runtime fails on this machine” is an observation with a particular environment. “I think a graph would make it easier” is a hypothesis. “I prefer one screen” is a preference whose importance may depend on the task. “We will preserve the current version until the replacement is ready” is a decision once the authorized person agrees. When the agent presents its synthesis, it should retain those distinctions. Turning every suggestion into a mandatory requirement overconstrains the design. Treating every requirement as negotiable removes the person's control over the outcome. The published Coding-Standards discovery procedure makes these distinctions explicit and asks what could make a technically correct implementation wrong for its intended use. It also preserves the boundary between discovery and implementation authority: research or a polished visual does not approve an unresolved design. This is a statement about the inspected policy, not evidence that every development session follows it. Discovery and Design at the inspected revision . Use examples to find the omitted rule People often recognize a bad result before they can formulate the rule that prevents it. Ask about a normal case, an interrupted case, and an awkward boundary. For acquisition, a normal case is a new resource becoming usable. An interrupted case is a cancelled operation. A boundary case is cancellation arriving after the bytes finish but before the resource is published. The last case exposes whether cancellation means “stop future work where possible,” “guarantee no publication,” or something else. Do not treat the first answer as an implementation detail the person should have known. The whole point of the conversation is to make the consequence visible. The agent can explain the possible behaviors and their costs, then ask which outcome matters. Examples should not become an exhaustive catalog. If ten examples all exercise the same distinction, another may add little. Seek a case that could change the rule. That is the difference between exploring the problem and making the conversation longer. Explain back without claiming certainty A useful synthesis describes what will be built, what the person will experience, and which consequences were added by the proposed solution. It also identifies the remaining question whose answer could change the direction. For example: the current version remains usable during preparation; the new version becomes visible only after verification; cancellation before publication preserves the old version; a missing runtime is reported rather than silently installed. The person can now challenge a picture of the behavior rather than inspect a list of internal tasks. Nuseibeh and Easterbrook describe requirements work as interpretive and iterative, with tacit knowledge limiting what interviews alone can uncover. Their roadmap supports combining conversation with observation, modeling, and revision. It does not promise complete understanding before implementation. Requirements Engineering A Roadmap . When conversation is enough A clear repair may need only one exchange. If a label shows the wrong unit, the correct unit is known, and no underlying semantic change is involved, extended discovery may delay a useful fix. A small patch can still require substantial discovery if it changes a coupled decision. Moving one success response earlier may alter what multiple consumers assume about readiness. The size of the diff does not measure the amount of shared understanding required. For your own task, identify the next question that could materially change the outcome, design, scope, or acceptance. If there is none, explain the direction and proceed within the available authority. If there is one, resolve it through a question, a source check, or a small experiment. The conversation should remain responsive while that investigation happens.

title: 3 Investigate before committing
text: 3 Investigate before committing Research becomes useful engineering work when a finding can change a live decision. Without that connection, it can produce a large collection of facts while leaving the actual uncertainty untouched. In our running example, the team is considering a new publication mechanism for acquired resources. Before designing it, someone should determine whether the existing API already preserves the old resource until a new candidate is ready. A familiar method name is not enough. Its contract, callers, state transitions, and failure behavior matter. The investigation may reveal that the existing mechanism fits. It may expose a narrow missing operation. Or it may show that the current abstraction confuses transfer completion with consumer readiness. Those outcomes lead to different amounts of work. Give research a decision and a stopping condition A useful brief has four elements: the question, the decision affected, the evidence needed, and the condition under which further investigation would stop changing the choice. For example: Determine whether the current resource API can publish a verified candidate while preserving existing readers of the old version. Inspect its contract and two actual callers. Exercise the failure boundary if the code does not establish it clearly. If the API already provides this behavior on supported storage, reuse it; otherwise describe the smallest missing promise. The brief is bounded without demanding a predetermined answer. It does not ask the investigator to “research acquisition architecture” indefinitely. It names what evidence would support reuse and what would justify a change. A stopping condition is not a timer that makes uncertainty disappear. It is an account of what the decision needs. If the missing evidence remains consequential, report the gap. If further detail would not change the selected reversible step, proceed and retain the limitation. Investigate the system as it exists now Puma's architectural discussions emphasize the danger of treating an old integration assumption as a current requirement. A consumer designed around an earlier API may need updating rather than forcing the provider to restore a now-unnecessary behavior. The general lesson is to inspect the current boundary before proposing a repair. Start with the actual entry point. Follow the successful path, then the error and cancellation paths. Identify what callers rely on and which facts are merely accidental. Read the relevant tests, but distinguish their assertions from observed execution. A test file can explain the intended contract even when it has not been run in the current environment. Sillito, Murphy, and De Volder's observational work identified programmers' questions ranging from finding a starting point to understanding relationships across code. Search results often needed integration before they answered the real question. The study is not an optimal-search recipe, but it supports describing the relationship you need to understand rather than equating investigation with locating a symbol. Questions Programmers Ask During Software Evolution Tasks . Treat existing implementation as a constraint with a price Current code constrains a change because compatibility, migration, and maintenance cost are real. It is not necessarily immutable. A design that exists for historical reasons may be the very thing preventing the intended outcome. Consider three possibilities. The desired behavior can fit the current interface directly. It can fit after a narrow refactor. Or accommodating it would perpetuate a misleading abstraction, making replacement worthwhile. Investigation should give enough evidence to compare these paths. “This is how the system works” is a description, not a complete argument for retaining it. The same applies to an external library. Check what it actually guarantees. A cancellation method might request cancellation without waiting for resource release. A version number may correlate with a capability without defining it. A provider may expose a common format while requiring distinct runtime support. Verify the relevant promise rather than infer it from a category label. Bryan Cantrill’s published Oxide discussion offers a useful distinction. He describes a familiar kernel task deliberately selected to favor the agent, and two subtle defects he needed to correct. That is expert-supervised delegation of a largely understood solution, not open-ended design discovery. His estimate of the time he would have needed without AI is not a control condition. The comparison reminds us to identify which uncertainty the agent is actually being asked to resolve. Engineering Rigor in the LLM Age , especially 07:01–14:56. Keep research from blocking the conversation Puma wants background research to proceed while the main agent continues discussing the problem. That can work when the handoff preserves decision ownership. A research task returns evidence, alternatives, and limitations; it does not silently replace the shared direction. The lead should integrate findings as soon as they matter. “The API already supplies the readiness boundary we need” is actionable. A long report that arrives after the plan has committed to a replacement is less useful. Conversely, an unresolved question should remain visible rather than be filled with an optimistic assumption merely to keep the conversation flowing. Parallel research is often easier to divide than parallel implementation. One investigator can inspect API semantics while another checks platform support. Their findings can still conflict, especially if they examined different versions. Record the revision or documentation version so the disagreement can be reconciled. Choose an experiment when reading stops helping Sometimes the cheapest evidence is a small reversible implementation. If a library's behavior is unclear, a minimal characterization test may be more informative than another hour of documentation. The experiment should state what it is testing and what it does not establish. A local process-kill test can examine cleanup after process termination. It does not prove resilience to power loss. A prototype on one filesystem can expose a flaw but cannot establish all supported platforms. An experiment becomes misleading when its result is promoted beyond the conditions exercised. Before your next investigation, write the decision it can change. Afterward, return the finding in that same form: what was inspected, what was observed, what conclusion follows, and what remains uncertain. Research is complete enough when the next commitment has a defensible basis, not when there are no more documents to read.

title: 4 Make the emerging design visible
text: 4 Make the emerging design visible A conversation unfolds one sentence at a time. A design often depends on relationships that must be considered together. Who owns a resource while another task is using it? Which state permits publication? Which unanswered question affects two competing approaches? A suitable visual can keep those relationships available while the conversation moves on. Puma's proposal for discovery includes a local page maintained alongside the discussion. Its purpose is to show the emerging picture: findings, open questions, choices, and relevant relationships. It should help participants notice a mismatch before a formal plan makes it look settled. The page is useful only if its representation fits the question. Choose what the reader needs to notice A state diagram can clarify which transitions are valid. An ownership map can show who retains a resource after a caller disappears. A sequence view can distinguish the order of events. An interface mockup can expose the words a person will see. A comparison table can put alternatives against the same criteria. For acquisition, a progress bar alone may conceal the distinction between transfer and readiness. A better discussion aid could show: Visible state What is true What the consumer may do Transferring Some candidate bytes are being acquired Continue using the old published version Checking Transfer has finished; readiness is unresolved Continue using the old version Ready The agreed checks and publication step have completed Resolve and use the new version Preparation failed This candidate cannot be published Inspect the reason; retain the previous usable version This is a proposed product contract, not a universal acquisition lifecycle. It makes assumptions available for discussion. Someone may object that consumers need simultaneous access to both versions, or that there is no previous version. That objection improves the model. Show uncertainty without making the page unreadable A live visual can accidentally look more authoritative than the discussion behind it. Clean typography and complete-looking boxes suggest that the design has been decided. If an option is provisional, say so near the option. If a finding depends on a particular version, keep the version available with the source. Avoid turning uncertainty into a sea of warning badges. Distinguish the few unresolved points that affect a decision from background details. A useful page might have a current proposal, two open material questions, and a small evidence list. It need not contain every sentence of the conversation. The page also needs a clear owner. If several agents rewrite it independently, they may merge incompatible assumptions into a polished composite. Puma's discovery design assigns a separate author to the visual while the lead owns synthesis and decisions. The benefit is coherent editing, but the arrangement still has a cost: the author must receive current information, and stale representations must be corrected promptly. A prototype answers a particular question Houde and Hill distinguish prototypes by what they investigate: a product's role, its look and feel, or its implementation. The distinction is useful because apparent completeness in one dimension can conceal absence in another. A convincing interface can say little about resource safety; a robust backend probe can say little about whether a person understands the result. What Do Prototypes Prototype . For our example, a mockup asks whether “Transfer complete, preparing for use” is understandable. A failure-injection test asks whether a candidate rejected before publication leaves the old version usable. A lost acknowledgment after publication is a different case: the transition may already have committed, so reconcile the uncertain result instead of assuming rollback. Chapter 25 returns to that boundary. Both are valuable. Neither replaces the other. Sometimes making the prototype changes the intended outcome. Mitchell Hashimoto's account of a Ghostty update feature starts with a bounded UI investigation and discovers preferences through the prototype. A later implementation works but conflates concerns; he changes the model and continues. The account supports intent and boundaries while challenging any rigid idea that intent must be completely discovered before construction. It is a first-person case with a linked change, not a controlled productivity comparison. Vibing a Non-Trivial Ghostty Feature . Preserve access beyond the visual A diagram should have readable labels and a textual account of its central claim. People may use screen readers, small screens, monochrome printouts, or slow connections. A relationship that exists only as a colored line may be difficult to inspect or cite later. Keep the important decision in a durable record once it is made. The visual can remain an explanatory view, but it should not become a competing authority whose outdated boxes contradict the plan. The cost of a live page rises when it duplicates information that must be changed in several places. For a current design discussion, choose one question a visual could answer. Make the smallest representation that exposes it. Ask someone to explain the proposed behavior from the view. Where their explanation differs, investigate whether the defect lies in the design, the labels, or an unstated assumption. The success criterion is improved understanding of that question, not an impressive page.

title: 5 Choose among meaningful alternatives
text: 5 Choose among meaningful alternatives An agent can often produce several architectures on request. That does not mean the alternatives expose a real decision. Three diagrams with different service names may conceal the same tradeoff, while one apparently minor difference in ownership changes the entire failure behavior. The point of alternatives is to reveal consequences that matter to the intended outcome. Compare the same problem For the resource system, consider three approaches. Reuse the existing publication API if it already provides the required readiness semantics. Add a narrow operation if transfer and publication are currently conflated. Introduce a shared acquisition layer if several actual consumers need the same identity and lifecycle contract. These options differ in scope, migration cost, and the responsibilities they centralize. Compare them against the same scenarios: a successful replacement, a failed readiness check, cancellation during finalization, an existing reader holding the old version, and a restart after an uncertain result. Do not let each option choose its own favorable criteria. A reusable layer should answer the same immediate usability requirement as a direct implementation. A small patch should account for any repeated lifecycle logic it leaves behind. The comparison should make costs visible on both sides. The Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method formalizes evaluation around quality scenarios, risks, sensitivity points, and tradeoffs. A small option note can borrow that reasoning without pretending to be a complete ATAM evaluation. The full method carries a process cost that may be inappropriate for a small reversible change. ATAM Method for Architecture Evaluation . Include the option of doing less A simpler design must be a legitimate outcome. If the consumer can tolerate restarting an interrupted download, resumable transfer may not belong in the first release. If only one application needs the behavior, a local implementation may be sufficient. If the existing interface fits, the best result of discovery may be a decision not to add another abstraction. Doing less is not automatically simpler over the whole lifecycle. Duplicating a subtle publication rule across three consumers may reduce today's diff while increasing tomorrow's risk. The relevant question is which complexity is necessary now, which is a demonstrated common need, and which is merely anticipated. An alternative should therefore include its likely point of reconsideration. “Use the current API until a second consumer needs a different retention policy” is more informative than “keep it simple.” It tells future developers what evidence would reopen the decision. Make consequences understandable A requester may approve an option because it meets every stated requirement, yet be surprised by an unstated consequence. A shared service may need to remain running. A local cache may retain data longer than expected. Automatic runtime selection may use more disk space. A stronger consistency rule may reduce concurrency. Explain these consequences in terms of behavior, not just implementation. “This keeps the old version available while preparing the new one, at the cost of temporarily storing both” is easier to judge than a storage-class diagram alone. Sometimes the consequence belongs to someone other than the requester. A change that makes contributions easier may increase maintainer review work. An agent-friendly interface may require another component to own retries or cleanup. Include the receiving party's needs rather than optimizing only the caller's experience. Do not manufacture numerical certainty A weighted score can help when criteria are genuinely comparable and the weights have an agreed meaning. It can also disguise judgment. Giving maintainability eight points and complexity six points does not measure either property. Use numbers where there is a basis: measured startup time, memory use under a stated workload, migration steps, or a known license cost. Use reasoned comparisons where there is not. State the uncertainty instead of converting it to an arbitrary decimal. Requirements framing itself can affect the search. Mohanani, Turhan, and Ralph's two experiments found less original but more practical concepts under requirements-oriented framing than ideas-oriented framing. Their paper-design tasks and samples limit transfer to agent engineering. The useful implication is to distinguish genuine obligations from tentative ideas, not to pretend every constraint is optional. Requirements Framing Affects Design Creativity . Record the choice at the right scale A compact decision record can retain the context, selected approach, alternatives, and consequences. It should explain the surprising part of the choice. If the obvious existing operation was reused without controversy, a sentence in the task record may suffice. If a shared boundary is being introduced, a durable record is more valuable. Michael Nygard's architecture-decision proposal uses short records with context, decision, status, and consequences, retaining superseded choices. It is an early practitioner account rather than measured proof of effectiveness. Its practical appeal is that future readers can understand why a choice made sense without reconstructing the entire discussion. Documenting Architecture Decisions . Choose one design decision in your current work. Describe two materially different viable approaches, or explain why only one meets the constraints. Compare them through the same concrete scenario. State the selected behavior, its cost, and the observation that would justify reconsidering it. That record is enough if it allows another developer to challenge the decision intelligently.

title: 6 Model the domain before choosing abstractions
text: Part 2 Shape the software around its problem The next chapters turn intended behavior into concepts, ownership, and boundaries. The running example acquires more precision only where a distinction changes what the system must do. 6 Model the domain before choosing abstractions A domain model earns its place when it helps explain a behavior that would otherwise remain ambiguous. It is not a list of nouns waiting to become classes. In the acquisition example, a person asks for one resource, a transfer is attempted, candidate bytes appear locally, checks run, and a consumer eventually receives something usable. Calling all of these “the download” is convenient until one stage succeeds and another fails. Then the system needs distinctions that its vocabulary has concealed. Start with examples. The same resource can be requested twice. One attempt can fail while another succeeds. Two artifacts may represent different versions. A candidate can exist without being ready. A published version can remain in use while a replacement is prepared. These statements reveal identity and lifecycle questions before any architecture is selected. Distinguish things that change independently A resource identity answers which thing is wanted. An attempt answers which effort to obtain it is being discussed. A candidate answers what is locally present but not yet accepted. A published resource answers what a consumer may currently use. Those concepts need not become four services or four classes. A small implementation may represent them with a few records and functions. The important point is that the system can express their different states without contradictory meanings. Consider an attempt identifier used as a permanent resource identifier. It seems adequate while every request succeeds once. When an attempt is retried, the application may create a second identity for the same resource. Alternatively, if every retry reuses one mutable record, historical events may become impossible to distinguish. The correct choice depends on what callers must be able to refer to and what records must preserve. A vocabulary table can expose the problem: Concept Remains the same when Changes when Requested resource A transfer is retried for the same selected identity The selected identity or version changes Acquisition attempt One attempt moves through its lifecycle A new attempt is admitted Candidate artifact Checks examine the same candidate bytes The candidate is replaced or reconstructed Published reference Existing readers retain the agreed version Publication deliberately changes the reference The table states an illustrative contract. It is not a claim that all products should use these exact identities. Name the rule before the object An invariant is a condition the system must preserve across relevant transitions. “An unverified candidate is never advertised as ready” is one. “Cancelling one consumer does not cancel another consumer's continuing demand” might be another if acquisition is shared. An invariant tells you something about a boundary. If several fields must change together to preserve it, they may need one consistency owner. If unrelated changes do not affect it, they may not belong in that owner's responsibility. Evans's domain-driven design reference connects shared language, identity, bounded contexts, and consistency rules. These ideas are useful for asking where a meaning is valid and who enforces a rule. They do not require a microservice per bounded context or a class for every concept. Domain Driven Design Reference . A framework can then implement the model. It should not silently supply the model's meaning. A database row, asynchronous task, or HTTP request may be a convenient representation, but its technical lifetime need not match the domain object's lifetime. Much later complexity comes from assuming that it does. Test the vocabulary against disagreement Ask two people to describe what happens when transfer completes but publication fails. If one says the resource is complete and the other says it is unavailable, they may be using “complete” for different events. Resolve the distinction before making the status field more elaborate. The same method applies to agents. A task may be assigned, admitted, running, awaiting input, or finished at a harness level. None automatically means its requested outcome has been accepted. If a single state called done serves all those meanings, downstream code will invent its own interpretation. Domain modeling is therefore also interface work. The words in a tool response teach the caller how to act. A misleading word can create a bug even when the underlying data is accurate. Resist the urge to complete the ontology There is always another distinction you could represent. The useful stopping point is the set needed for current behavior, meaningful variation, and known failure boundaries. If a proposed concept cannot explain a scenario, enforce a rule, or support an actual decision, it may not belong yet. For an exercise, take three status names from a system you maintain. For each, write what is true, what the caller may do, and one situation it must exclude. Then identify a pair whose meanings overlap or conflict. Repair the vocabulary before adding more states. The result may be a new concept, a simpler name, or the removal of an unnecessary distinction.

title: 7 Make ownership and lifecycles explicit
text: 7 Make ownership and lifecycles explicit Ownership becomes interesting when something disappears. A caller disconnects, an agent is cancelled, a process restarts, or a request times out. The system still has resources, effects, and obligations. Who owns them now? Three meanings of ownership often become entangled. Object ownership concerns who keeps a value alive. Operational responsibility concerns who must finish or clean up work. Authority concerns who may decide that an action should happen. A reference-counted pointer can solve the first while leaving the other two unresolved. In the resource example, a consumer may request acquisition without owning the shared transfer. A service may own the transfer without being authorized to select a substitute resource. A background effect may retain a workspace after the requesting future has been dropped. The design needs to express these differences. Follow the effect rather than the requester A concrete Pumas change makes the issue visible. In the inspected draft acquisition work, a blocking effect could continue after its asynchronous waiter and callback disappeared. The registered effect did not itself retain the workspace reservation. The repair captured the workspace inside that effect, so the activity still able to touch the resource retained its claim until it returned. The associated regression uses an actual exclusive lock, holds the blocking work, cancels the waiter, and attempts a competing acquisition of the lock. The competing handle must fail while the effect remains active and succeed after it finishes. Source and test assertions were inspected, and local results were recorded by the project. This is bounded evidence for the ownership rule, not comprehensive production or cross-platform qualification. Repair ; regression at the inspected head . The general question is simple: which activity can still produce a side effect? That activity needs the relevant resource claim, even if the person who originally asked for it has stopped waiting. Describe transitions with obligations A list of states is not enough. Each transition should explain its precondition, effect, authority, and outstanding obligation. For example, moving a candidate from checking to ready may require all readiness checks to pass, publication to occur, and the consumer reference to resolve. Moving from transferring to cancel requested may only record intent to stop. The latter state must not imply that the worker has stopped touching its workspace. A useful transition record could say: Before: candidate exists, no ready reference has been published Decision owner: acquisition service under the caller's admitted request Required evidence: specified checks passed for this candidate identity Effect: publish the ready reference After: consumers may use the candidate; cleanup responsibility for superseded storage is separately defined The cleanup clause prevents a common omission. Successful publication may leave work behind. If the caller's response ends the only lifetime that retained cleanup responsibility, success becomes a resource leak. Shared demand changes cancellation Suppose two consumers need the same resource. Cancelling one consumer's request need not mean cancelling the shared work. The system may remove that consumer's demand while continuing for the other. This is a different domain from one request owning one task. Reusing a cancellation token without examining its meaning can make the first departing consumer disrupt everyone else. Conversely, never cancelling shared work can waste resources after all demand disappears. Model the demand separately when the distinction matters. Decide who counts active consumers, how stale demand is retired, and what happens when new demand arrives during shutdown. There may be races that require one serialized owner or a compare-and-update operation. The solution should follow the invariant, not a preference for a particular concurrency primitive. Make uncertain outcomes expressible A timeout can mean that the observer stopped waiting, not that the operation failed. If publication may already have happened, blindly retrying can duplicate effects. The next action should usually inspect authoritative state or use an operation whose retry semantics account for identity. An explicit uncertain state can be useful, but it should have a resolution path. A system that records uncertainty forever without allowing reconciliation has described the problem without making it operable. For your own project, choose one resource that outlives a request: a process, file lock, network operation, temporary directory, or agent task. Draw the lifetimes of the caller, effect, and cleanup owner. Terminate the caller in the model. If an obligation has no remaining owner, the design is incomplete. If several owners can independently release the same resource, inspect that boundary too.

title: 8 Keep the necessary complexity separate
text: 8 Keep the necessary complexity separate Simple and easy describe different things. A familiar framework may be easy to use while entangling several decisions. An unfamiliar design may require learning but allow each concern to be understood independently. Neither familiarity nor brevity is a sufficient measure of simplicity. Puma's standards use this distinction to resist arbitrary proxies such as file count, type count, or call count. The relevant question is whether independent concerns can be understood and changed independently. A coherent module can be substantial because the problem itself is substantial. Splitting it into many fragments may move complexity into coordination without reducing it. Code Design at the inspected revision . Locate the coupling that hurts Imagine one function that downloads bytes, chooses a runtime, updates a catalog, renders progress text, and deletes old files. It may be easy to call. Its internal decisions are entangled if changing a presentation label requires understanding publication order, or if supporting a new provider requires changing cleanup semantics. Do not respond by extracting every step into a service. First identify the change that should be independent. Presentation might depend on a stable status model. Provider transfer details might sit behind an acquisition contract. Publication and catalog update may need to remain together because they preserve one invariant. The design should follow the actual dependencies. Two operations occurring at different times do not necessarily belong in different owners. Two functions with similar code do not necessarily express the same rule. Parnas's classic modularity comparison asks which design decisions should be hidden, rather than simply dividing a program by processing steps. It remains useful as a question about change: what should be able to vary without forcing unrelated consumers to vary? It is a design argument and worked comparison, not a theorem that more modules improve performance. On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules . Count the complexity you add A refactor can remove one coupling and add several new concepts: an interface, registry, lifecycle, configuration format, and error translation layer. Those may be justified, but they are costs. For the running example, extracting transfer adapters may make provider variation easier. If it also introduces a global plugin service, dynamic registration, remote discovery, and version negotiation for a single fixed provider, the abstraction may exceed the demonstrated need. A useful explanation says both what becomes easier and what becomes harder. “The readiness rule has one owner, so adding a provider no longer changes publication. The cost is that each provider must translate its progress and errors into this contract.” That is more informative than calling the result clean. The opposite problem is under-modeling. A dozen conditionals may seem smaller than an explicit state representation, but if they collectively encode a lifecycle that nobody can explain, the design is not simple in the relevant sense. Fewer declarations can conceal more mental work. Separate policy from mechanism when they vary for different reasons A transfer mechanism moves bytes. A retention policy decides how long to keep them. A scheduler decides when work may run. A readiness policy decides what a consumer can rely on. These may be implemented near one another, but their reasons for changing differ. Not every separation needs a public interface. A private function or record can make a distinction clear without creating a new compatibility obligation. Public boundaries should be introduced where actual callers need them. The level of abstraction also matters. A generic event system can represent every lifecycle transition, but may obscure the specific rules that make acquisition correct. A domain-specific operation may be easier to reason about because it narrows the permitted combinations. Review a design through a change scenario Choose a plausible change: add a provider, preserve a previous version, support cancellation during verification, or change the progress display. List the decisions that must be understood to make it safely. Then ask which dependencies are necessary. If presentation depends on the meaning of ready, that is legitimate. If presentation depends on the provider's temporary filename scheme, the boundary may be leaking incidental detail. A useful refactor reduces the number of unrelated decisions that must be held in mind for that change. It need not reduce lines or files. Test it by explaining the before and after paths to another developer. If the explanation simply substitutes five new abstractions for one old confusion, reconsider the design.

title: 9 Design boundaries that can hold
text: 9 Design boundaries that can hold A boundary is a set of promises between parts of a system. Its value depends on whether those promises remain meaningful when implementations vary, fail, or evolve. An interface can have a neat schema and still be a poor boundary. If callers must know a provider's private directory layout, retry timing, or database row ordering, the abstraction has not removed those dependencies. It has merely hidden them until something changes. Puma's ecosystem makes boundary design a recurring concern. Model management, inference execution, workflow orchestration, and application behavior have related responsibilities, but they should not automatically own one another's internal decisions. Begin with two actual caller situations For acquisition, one consumer might need a verified local artifact without running it. Another might need a model ready for a particular runtime. Those are related but different outcomes. If the API returns the same undifferentiated success for both, one caller may assume a stronger promise than the provider made. Write the contract in terms of what the caller can rely on. Which identity is returned? What does readiness include? Can the resource disappear while the caller uses it? Which failure is recoverable? What happens after the caller loses the response? A useful boundary also says what it does not promise when that omission affects action. A model manager may identify model-specific dependencies without guaranteeing that every inference backend supports them. A runtime adapter may establish its capabilities without choosing the user's preferred model. These are domain limits, not excuses for a vague interface. Probe the capability that matters A hardcoded version rule may be a convenient starting point, but version identity is not the same as capability. A newer runtime may preserve the required behavior. An older build may contain a backport. A provider's Python API may be distinct from the application's serving protocol. Before adding a compatibility check, identify the boundary being tested. Does the caller need a command, an output field, a loading behavior, or a lifecycle guarantee? Probe that property when feasible and report what was observed. A version label can remain useful context without becoming an unsupported gate. This approach has costs. A probe may be expensive, destructive, incomplete, or dependent on a model artifact. The design should choose a bounded check and retain uncertainty where appropriate. “Capability verified” must name the capability and conditions, not imply universal compatibility. Errors are part of the contract A caller needs to know what to do after failure. Compare “operation failed” with “candidate verification failed; the previous published version remains available; this attempt made no publication change.” The latter communicates state and next-step possibilities. Do not expose every internal exception as a public error type. Preserve distinctions that affect recovery, authority, or user understanding. A transient transfer interruption and an unsupported format may need different responses. Two internal parsing exceptions with the same caller consequence may not. An error can also be uncertain. If a response is lost after publication, the operation should offer a way to resolve the attempt's authoritative state. A retry without identity may be a new request; a retry bound to the original operation may be a continuation. The caller should not have to guess. Avoid encoding one consumer as the domain A shared layer can accidentally preserve the first application's schema as though it were universal. The second consumer then receives irrelevant fields or must mimic the first application's workflow to use the service. The remedy is not speculative generality. Inspect the demonstrated common need. Which identity, operation, or lifecycle is shared? Which fields belong to one application? A storage layer can expose durable records without inheriting every application concept stored in them. A boundary should make variation explicit where it is real and leave application-specific meaning with its owner. This is especially important when a shared engine is intended to serve agents that may otherwise infer undocumented requirements from examples. Andreas Kling’s Ladybird account describes a deliberately bounded JavaScript frontend migration, with an existing implementation used for differential comparison. Agreement with the reference was a concrete target, even where it postponed idiomatic cleanup. It also carried a limit: matching the old implementation can preserve old defects. His later account of restricting outside pull requests addresses another boundary, the maintainers’ ability to accept responsibility for changes. Producing technically plausible code and admitting it into a maintained browser are different outcomes. These are project-specific accounts, not a universal policy for generated contributions. Ladybird adopts Rust ; Changing How We Develop Ladybird . Exercise the boundary from outside Write a small consumer that uses only the documented contract. It should not import private modules or read hidden state. Make it handle normal success, a recoverable failure, and an uncertain result. If the consumer needs an undocumented fact, decide whether that fact belongs in the contract or whether the provider should absorb the detail. If the contract requires a sequence whose middle states are unsafe for ordinary callers, consider an intent-oriented operation with explicit choices. The strongest boundary is not the one with the fewest methods. It is the one whose promises callers can understand and whose owners can actually keep.

title: 10 Decide when to reuse refactor or replace
text: 10 Decide when to reuse refactor or replace Existing code deserves neither automatic preservation nor automatic suspicion. It represents working behavior, accumulated knowledge, and compatibility obligations. It may also encode assumptions that no longer fit the product. The decision to reuse, refactor, or replace should begin with a present problem. What behavior is missing? What change is unusually difficult? What failure recurs? What information must a developer understand that should have remained irrelevant? Without that problem, a redesign can become a preference disguised as necessity. Reuse requires semantic fit Two functions with similar names are not necessarily interchangeable. Reusing an API because it already exists can preserve the wrong readiness boundary or ownership rule. Conversely, writing a replacement because the old code is unfamiliar can discard a correct solution without evidence. For acquisition, inspect whether the existing operation preserves the old version during preparation and what its success response means. If it already satisfies the needed behavior, reuse may be the best outcome. If it almost fits, identify the missing promise before introducing another subsystem. Reuse also has an integration cost. Adapters, configuration, error translation, and lifecycle alignment can make a nominally free component expensive. Include those costs in the comparison rather than measuring only the implementation you avoid writing. Refactor to improve a named property A refactor should make a relevant change easier to understand or safer to perform while preserving required behavior. State that property before editing. “Separate provider transfer from publication so a new provider cannot alter readiness semantics” is a testable rationale. “Clean up the architecture” is too broad to guide a review. It does not tell a reviewer which complexity should disappear or what must remain stable. Research at Microsoft combined engineer reports with repository analysis and found varied benefits and costs around refactoring. A later study across 103 Java projects showed how mixed changes and attribution methods complicate claims about refactoring-related bugs. These studies do not make refactoring either harmless or inherently dangerous. They support evaluating the specific objective and separating observed association from cause. Refactoring Challenges and Benefits ; Differentiated Replication . For a practical change, preserve characterization tests where they capture important behavior. Add a test for the actual property the refactor is meant to improve when that property is executable. Some benefits, such as comprehensibility, need a different assessment: a reviewer should be able to explain the new ownership path without reconstructing unrelated decisions. Replacement needs a migration story A replacement can be justified when the old model makes the required behavior persistently awkward or unsafe. It still needs a path from current use to the new design. Who depends on the old contract? Can both versions coexist? How is stored data migrated? What makes rollback possible? Which compatibility behavior is genuinely required, and which exists only because nobody has removed it? A clean new component with an unexplained transition is not a complete solution. Migration can dominate the work. It can also reveal that a smaller refactor would have been sufficient. Avoid preserving compatibility indefinitely by default. Compatibility itself is code, testing, and conceptual overhead. But removing it should be an explicit decision grounded in actual consumers, rather than an assumption that no one needs it. Defer a capability without abandoning changeability Fowler's account of YAGNI distinguishes speculative features from practices that keep software changeable, such as refactoring and testing. His design-stamina discussion is explicitly a hypothesis, not a measured curve guaranteeing a payoff after a particular number of weeks. These distinctions help keep both extremes in view: premature infrastructure and avoidable decay. Yagni ; Design Stamina Hypothesis . For our example, resumable transfer may be a speculative capability. A clear publication boundary may already be necessary for today's cancellation behavior. Deferring the former does not justify entangling the latter. Make the decision reviewable Write a short note containing the current problem, evidence that the problem exists, the selected change, the behavior that must remain stable, migration costs, and the result that would show the work was worthwhile. Then include one credible alternative. It may be reuse with a small adapter, a narrower refactor, or deliberate deferral. If you cannot explain why that alternative is insufficient, the replacement proposal may not yet be ready. After the work, revisit the original claim. Did the change actually reduce the coupling, failure rate, or maintenance burden it targeted? If the answer is unknown, say so. A successful merge proves that a change entered the repository, not that its architectural promise was fulfilled.

title: 11 Learn through real applications
text: 11 Learn through real applications A useful product can also be a place to investigate an uncertain idea. Those roles should be distinguished without reducing the product to an experiment. A model-management application can provide a practical service while also letting engineers evaluate how different inference backends might work through a common API. A workflow or ledger component may be useful on its own while its lessons inform other work. Beginning experimentally does not make every current responsibility provisional. This matters because product users and researchers need different kinds of confidence. A user needs to know what works and what is supported. An investigation needs to know which hypothesis a particular observation addresses. Name the question inside the product Suppose a model-management application adds a second inference backend. The product outcome might be the ability to run a supported model through either backend. The research question might be whether a shared request representation can cover both without hiding important differences. Success for the product does not automatically answer the architectural question. The integration might work because of backend-specific exceptions that make the proposed common API unhelpful. Conversely, an unsuccessful prototype might still reveal a valuable boundary: generation parameters can be shared, while lifecycle or adapter dependencies need separate treatment. Write the product commitment and the investigative question separately. This lets the team learn without quietly weakening what users were promised. Transfer a lesson at the right level A workflow ledger that works for one application may demonstrate durable event recording but not the right information model for every application. An early conflict detector may demonstrate one guarded edit path without establishing reliable massive parallelism. A graph view may help answer one navigation question without replacing all text-based development. When transferring a lesson, identify what remained constant and what changed. The new system may have different concurrency, authority, latency, or retention requirements. A pattern is transferable only to the extent that its assumptions still hold. A proposed adaptation between systems is not a delivered integration. The systems may have different responsibilities and constraints; a diagram connecting them does not establish that the connection works. Make a prototype disposable in the right way Disposable does not mean careless. A prototype should preserve enough evidence to explain what was learned. It need not retain production-quality infrastructure that was irrelevant to the question. If the question is whether people understand a workflow without a node editor, a lightweight interface may be enough. If the question is whether a ledger can support deterministic reconstruction, a visual prototype alone is inadequate. Match the implementation effort to the uncertainty. Hashimoto's earlier account of building Ghostty emphasizes testable increments, frequent demonstrations, disposable scaffolding, and using the product to discover necessities. It offers a useful pre-agent comparison: many of these habits are durable engineering practice rather than new consequences of language models. My Approach to Building Large Technical Projects . Keep research from swallowing delivery An application can become a perpetual source of interesting foundational work. Each new requirement reveals another abstraction that could serve future products. The exploration may be valuable and still postpone the original usable outcome indefinitely. Define the next end-to-end result. What can a person do with the system after this slice that they cannot do now? Which unresolved idea blocks that result, and which can remain an experiment alongside it? The answer need not always favor the smallest demo. Some infrastructure is necessary for a dependable product. The important point is to make the tradeoff explicit rather than let architectural interest silently choose the priority. For a project containing research, create a two-column account: current product promises and open investigative questions. Take one proposed change and place its obligations in the appropriate column. If it belongs in both, explain how the product remains usable while the hypothesis is tested. That separation protects both honest learning and reliable delivery.

title: 12 Treat the agent as a real interface user
text: Part 3 Design software that agents can use An agent is a caller with its own discovery, feedback, and recovery needs. These chapters connect usable interfaces with authority and evidence, while keeping model judgment distinct from the conditions software can enforce. 12 Treat the agent as a real interface user An agent-facing interface has users with limited attention, incomplete knowledge, and predictable ways of making mistakes. Those users are not human, but the design questions remain recognizable. Can they discover the right operation? Can they understand what it does? Does the response tell them how to recover? Can they distinguish a successful action from a merely valid call? Puma treats these questions as central to the stack because agents are intended to consume and build the software. An API that is technically available but difficult for an agent to use is a product problem, not merely a prompting problem. Examine the whole interaction The interface includes more than the tool schema. It includes names, descriptions, available examples, discovery mechanisms, error messages, execution latency, and the state visible after an operation. Suppose an agent must find a model, inspect its requirements, choose a runtime, acquire artifacts, wait for readiness, and request inference. If each step returns ambiguous identifiers or hides the next valid action, the agent must reconstruct the protocol from scattered clues. A large context window does not make that reconstruction reliable or cheap. Observe a real interaction. Where does the agent guess? Where does it repeat a call because the response was unclear? Where does it retrieve an entire catalog to answer one question? Those observations suggest specific interface changes. “Make the tools better” does not. SWE-agent's experiments provide bounded evidence that tools and feedback can affect issue-resolution performance with a model held fixed. They support treating the interaction as a design variable. They do not establish one permanently optimal tool set for all models or repositories. SWE-agent . Make mistakes informative A schema error can be a useful teaching moment if it identifies the invalid field, the expected form, and the relevant constraint. A generic rejection may force the agent to try several guesses. Do not make an error response silently grant authority or recommend an unsafe action. Its job is to explain the boundary. If the requested operation is not allowed on the current revision, say which precondition failed. If a capability is absent, distinguish absence from a temporary failure. If the outcome is uncertain, provide a way to inspect the authoritative state. The response should match the caller's decision. An internal stack trace may help a maintainer but overwhelm an agent trying to determine whether retry is valid. Structured failure data and a concise explanation can serve both, with deeper diagnostics available when needed. Prefer a demonstrated improvement to a new layer An agent-first system does not automatically need a dedicated protocol for every action. Armin Ronacher's practical recommendations emphasize fast feedback, useful errors and logs, and application permission checks near the relevant operation. He often favors existing shell or database tools before adding MCP machinery. This is a first-person account, not a universal ranking, but it challenges the assumption that a new agent interface is inherently more usable. Agentic Coding Recommendations . For the resource example, a reliable command that returns stable identity and readiness information may be enough. A domain operation becomes valuable when it removes recurring choreography, centralizes a real invariant, or makes recovery understandable. The new layer should earn its cost through those effects. Evaluate outcomes rather than presentation alone A smaller catalog can reduce information load while making discovery harder. A compact response can omit a field needed for safe recovery. A friendly description can conceal a consequential default. Compare interfaces on the same tasks. Record whether the agent achieved the intended result, made an invalid or unauthorized attempt, recovered from a failure, and required human intervention. Count calls, latency, and information volume as explanatory measures, not substitutes for success. For an exercise, give an agent a task using an unfamiliar tool. Preserve the interaction. Identify one point where it lacked information needed for a decision. Change the interface or discovery path, then try a comparable task. A single improvement is not a general benchmark, but it can establish a concrete defect and a plausible repair. The objective is not to prevent every mistake through longer instructions. It is to make the system's important distinctions discoverable, its operations understandable, and its failures recoverable.

title: 13 Build interfaces around intent
text: 13 Build interfaces around intent An intent-oriented operation lets a caller request a meaningful outcome while the system owns the incidental steps required to achieve it. The idea is attractive because agents can otherwise spend many calls reconstructing a workflow that the software already understands. The danger is that a convenient operation can hide decisions the caller should control. “Make this model available” could mean download artifacts, choose a version, install a runtime, modify configuration, reserve memory, or start a process. Some of those may be required by the contract. Others may be surprising side effects. The operation is not well designed until those choices are explicit. Compress choreography without hiding authority Consider two interfaces. The first exposes every filesystem and catalog action. The caller must sequence them correctly and recover from partial failure. The second accepts a resource identity and readiness requirement, then performs the necessary acquisition and publication under a defined contract. The second can be simpler for callers because the provider owns a domain invariant. It should still expose consequential choices: allowed substitutions, retention behavior, whether runtime installation is authorized, and what counts as ready. An intent interface is therefore not a license for the system to infer every preference. It should reduce irrelevant representation knowledge while preserving the decisions that affect the user's outcome. Add the missing domain transition The standards engine provides a concrete example. Its authoring workflow could create initial policies for a new standard and revise existing policy scopes. But it lacked a supported way to register a new policy scope inside an existing standard. A legitimate domain transition was missing from the interface. The repair added a registration edit within the existing proposal mechanism. The author supplies the owner and policy identity and the intended scope. The engine owns placement, registry handling, ordering, and validation. The design did not require a raw file-edit API, another service, or a second graph. Inspected tests check preservation of existing content, stable treatment of identities, grouped validation, and failures that do not mutate the predecessor. Inspected registration tests and replay and mutation-resistance tests provide the direct examples. Historical reports record broader qualification; this book did not rerun it. Registration plan ; implementation . The lesson is about expressibility. A caller should be able to request the domain change it is authorized to make without learning incidental storage mechanics. Define the success boundary For acquisition, the operation might return a receipt identifying the attempt, selected resource, published artifact, and readiness claim. The receipt should not imply that all future uses will succeed. It establishes the bounded result promised by the operation. Partial progress should remain distinguishable. The bytes may be present while checks are pending. A runtime may be installed while loading fails. If the operation returns early, its response should represent an admitted or running task rather than final success. This matters for composability. A workflow engine may use the response to decide which node can run next. If it mistakes admission for completion, the convenience API has exported a race into every consumer. Make retry semantics part of the operation A caller that loses a response needs to know whether repeating the call continues the same intended action or starts another. Stable operation identity can help, but the meaning must be defined. An idempotency key that silently accepts different parameters is dangerous; a key that never expires may create its own retention and collision problems. A useful design distinguishes same intent retried, changed intent, and a new attempt after a terminal result. It provides an authoritative lookup when the outcome is uncertain. The exact implementation can vary, but the caller should not have to infer these semantics from timing. Retain an escape path at the correct level High-level operations do not remove the need for diagnostics or specialized use. A caller may need to inspect why readiness failed or request a narrower artifact-only outcome. Provide those capabilities deliberately rather than exposing internal mutation as an emergency workaround. The test for an intent interface is whether a new caller can use it correctly from its contract. Ask that caller to perform normal acquisition, handle a missing capability, and resolve a lost response. If each path requires private knowledge, the interface has not yet absorbed the choreography it claims to own.

title: 14 Connect standards knowledge and decisions
text: 14 Connect standards knowledge and decisions A standards document can contain valuable guidance and still be difficult to use at the moment it matters. An agent may receive too much irrelevant material, miss the rule that changes its decision, or apply a specialized workflow to an ordinary repair. Puma's Coding-Standards work treats this as an interface and information-model problem. The standards are not merely a collection of agent skills. They include relationships, policy identities, routing, and qualification mechanisms intended to make relevant guidance usable by agents. The distinction matters because publishing a paragraph and making it discoverable are different changes. Route by the decision being made A request with material uncertainty about the intended behavior may need discovery even if the eventual patch is small. A request to investigate a known technical behavior may need a bounded research path without reopening product design. A clear low-impact repair may need neither a long plan nor a complex coordination protocol. Routing should distinguish these situations through facts relevant to the decision. It should not rely only on labels such as small, complex, or multiple agents. Those labels can correlate with a need without defining it. For example, concurrent research does not necessarily create competing edits to shared authority. Several agents can investigate independently while one person integrates the findings. A stale-proposal protocol becomes relevant when independently prepared changes may be applied against a state that has changed. Participant count alone does not establish that risk. A relationship graph is still a model A graph can connect a topic, policy, workflow, consumer, and evidence record. Those edges make useful questions possible: what guidance applies here, which consumers could be affected by this revision, and what qualification supports it? The graph does not discover all real relationships automatically. A declared consumer may be missing. A relationship may be stale. A route may be too broad. The implementation should make these possibilities inspectable rather than present the graph as complete because it is machine-readable. The inspected discovery publication includes policy scopes and consumer relationships as well as prose. That supports a claim that the procedure is registered, not a claim that every agent selects it correctly or that all downstream behavior has been verified. This distinction becomes important when evaluating any executable standards system. Registered policy scopes , declared consumer relationships . Provide the right amount of context More instructions can increase cost and distraction. Less context can omit a crucial constraint. The design problem is relevance, not a universal preference for long or short prompts. The inspected AGENTS.md study compared repository context arrangements across issue-solving tasks. Generated context increased average inference cost, while average success differences from no context were not statistically significant. Developer-written files did better than generated ones but did not show a significant average gain over no file. The tested settings do not establish the value of Puma's scoped engine; they are a useful counterweight to assuming that added instructions must help. Evaluating AGENTS.md . A practical standards interface should let the agent discover relevant guidance and inspect supporting detail when needed. It should also make omissions visible enough to correct. A small catalog that routes to the wrong rule is not an improvement merely because it uses fewer tokens. Distinguish application from qualification A rule can be available, selected, understood, applied, and effective. Those are separate claims. A route test may show that a given fact pattern selects Planning. A structural check may show that a policy has a valid identity. A conversation review may show that an agent explained a consequence. An outcome observation may show that the resulting product fit the user's intent. No single check substitutes for all the others. This is where standards work can become overbuilt.
