If every relationship needs elaborate proof before any ordinary change can proceed, the infrastructure may obstruct its own purpose. The system should preserve the distinctions that matter without turning all uncertainty into a blocking state. Exercise the guidance as an interface Take three tasks: a small clear repair, a small ambiguous request, and a larger but well-understood implementation. For each, predict which guidance should apply and why. Then observe the actual route and the agent's use of the result. If the route is wrong, identify the missing or misleading fact. If the route is correct but the agent misuses the rule, inspect presentation and examples. If the rule is followed but the outcome is poor, revise the rule or its applicability rather than celebrating compliance. The standards should help people and agents make better decisions. Their own design therefore needs the same outcome-based scrutiny as the software they govern.

title: 15 Separate probabilistic judgment from deterministic control
text: 15 Separate probabilistic judgment from deterministic control A model can propose a design, interpret an error, or suggest a patch. A system can deterministically enforce a revision precondition, check a permission, or reject an invalid state transition. Combining these capabilities is useful, but their responsibilities should remain clear. A deterministic check is reliable only about the predicate it actually evaluates. It does not make an unchecked proposition true. Separate four questions When an agent proposes a change, ask four different questions: Is the proposal structurally valid? Is this actor authorized to perform it? Are the relevant state and revision preconditions still true? Does the result serve the intended outcome? A schema can help answer the first. An authority mechanism can answer the second within its policy. A revision guard can answer the third. The fourth usually requires a combination of domain checks, tests, observation, and judgment. Confusing these questions creates false confidence. A valid JSON object can request the wrong action. An authorized operation can use a stale assumption. A revision-correct patch can violate an invariant the controller does not know about. Construct a two-stage failure In the illustrative resource system, an agent proposes changing publication behavior against revision A. Another change creates revision B before application. The controller rejects the stale proposal. That is useful: the proposal was prepared against assumptions that may no longer hold. Now prepare a proposal against B that passes the revision check but announces ready before verification finishes. The controller accepts it if readiness semantics are not among its predicates. The first guard worked correctly; the system still needs another way to detect the second defect. This exercise prevents a common overstatement. “Guarded application” describes a boundary. It is not synonymous with correct implementation. CaMeL provides a related architectural comparison by separating model processing from policy-enforcing interpretation and tracking data provenance. Its guarantees depend on a defined threat model and correctly specified policies. It does not solve every misleading-text problem or remove the need to establish what the policy should be. CaMeL . Put the rule with its owner A resource owner should enforce the lifecycle conditions that make its resource safe to use. A caller can validate its own inputs, but duplicating the authoritative rule across callers invites disagreement. For publication, the component that makes a candidate visible should check the relevant readiness state at that boundary. A user interface disabling a button may help ordinary interaction, but it is not sufficient if other callers can invoke the operation. The same principle applies to agent coordination. A proposal may describe an allowed write set, but the applying mechanism must enforce the relevant scope if correctness depends on it. A prompt instruction and an execution boundary provide different kinds of assurance. Do not centralize every rule in one universal controller. Different owners may have distinct authority and consistency responsibilities. The design should make the handoff explicit rather than pretend a global validator can infer every domain condition. Keep probabilistic information attributable A model's estimate that a task is low risk may be useful input. It should remain an estimate, not silently become a verified fact. A generated explanation can help a reviewer understand a proposal, but it should not replace the actual diff or observed test result. When uncertain judgment influences an action, record which claim was made, by whom or by which system, and which checks followed. This makes later disagreement tractable. It also prevents an interface from laundering a model's confidence into an authoritative status. Decide what happens when evidence is missing Some operations can proceed reversibly while uncertainty is investigated. Others require a pause because the unresolved condition affects a consequential action. That choice is part of the product's policy and risk model. A controller that rejects every incomplete description may make ordinary work impossible. A controller that accepts every plausible proposal may leave critical authority to generation. The useful middle is explicit: which conditions are mandatory at this boundary, which are advisory, and how does a rejected operation become actionable? For your system, list one check in each of the four categories. Then create a proposal that passes three while failing the fourth. If the team cannot explain the outcome, the boundary is probably relying on a vague idea of validation rather than a precise set of promises.

title: 16 Record what happened and why
text: 16 Record what happened and why A record is useful when it lets someone answer a question that would otherwise remain uncertain. What was requested? Which interface was used? What response was returned? Which decision authorized a change? What state was actually observed afterward? Puma's interest in ledgers and information graphs grows from these questions. The ambition is broader than logging errors. It includes preserving the relationship between intent, decisions, execution, and evidence so later agents and people can inspect it. The first design task is deciding what the record can honestly claim. Separate observation from interpretation Suppose an agent calls an acquisition operation and receives a timeout. An observer can record the request and response. It cannot infer from that exchange alone that acquisition failed, that publication did not occur, or that the caller was wrong to make the request. Those conclusions require other evidence. A later state lookup may show publication completed. A policy engine may report that the operation was unauthorized. A reviewer may conclude that the requested identity did not match the intended resource. These should be attributable additions, not retroactive replacements for the observed interaction. Puma's proposed recorder design makes this distinction important: recording communication does not require the observer to decide whether an operation was malformed or semantically valid. If an interface supplies information about what should be retained, that is a separate contract. The proposal also keeps observer reporting out of the evaluated agent's input, so the act of recording does not silently become additional feedback. This is a stated design requirement, not a claim that every recorder implementation already has it. A minimal event can be enough For the running example, a useful record might contain an event identity, time, actor identity, operation identity, target resource, relevant revision, and a reference to the request or result. A state observation should identify what was observed and when. A decision record should identify its authority and the alternatives or consequences it preserves. Do not add fields simply because a graph can store them. Each field creates collection, retention, interpretation, and migration obligations. A record of every byte may be expensive and may retain information nobody needs. The W3C provenance model offers vocabulary for entities, activities, agents, derivation, and attribution. It can help distinguish relationships without prescribing one storage design. A vocabulary is not evidence that the resulting graph is complete or useful for a particular development task. PROV Data Model . Reasons are claims too A person or model may explain why a choice was made. Preserve that explanation as an attributed account. Do not assume it captures every influence on the decision. Research on reasoning faithfulness shows that model explanations can omit information that influenced answers in the studied settings. Those experiments do not establish a universal omission rate for coding agents. They do justify keeping a generated rationale distinct from the observable interaction and resulting state. Reasoning Models Do Not Always Say What They Think . This distinction makes records more useful, not less. A reviewer can compare an asserted reason with the available evidence and identify a mismatch. If the record treats rationale as unquestionable truth, it prevents that comparison. Preserve the question across changing representations An interface version can change field names or available operations. A plan can be superseded. A source artifact can move. If the record only stores mutable labels, later readers may reconstruct the wrong context. Stable identities and revision references help, but they should be used where they support a real reconstruction need. Not every transient observation requires a permanent globally meaningful identifier. The design should balance traceability with the cost of maintaining identity across the system. A ledger also needs to distinguish correction from erasure. A later observation may resolve an uncertain outcome without making the original uncertainty disappear. Keeping both lets someone understand what was knowable at the time and why the next action was reasonable. Test the record by asking a difficult question Take one completed operation and try to reconstruct it using only the retained evidence. Which request led to it? What authority applied? Which implementation revision ran? What result was observed? What remains unknowable? Then remove one event from the exercise. Can the record detect the gap, or does it silently imply continuity? A long log that cannot expose missing coverage may be less trustworthy than a short record that states its limits. The purpose of provenance is not to make every decision look justified afterward. It is to preserve enough context that a later reader can understand, challenge, and improve the work.

title: 17 Write plans that preserve intent
text: Part 4 Turn shared understanding into coordinated work A design must survive handoffs, parallel work, and new information. The next chapters develop compact plans, development boundaries, task ownership, and revision paths that preserve the outcome without imposing the same machinery on every change. 17 Write plans that preserve intent A plan can be detailed enough to keep an agent busy and still be missing the reason for the work. “Add a downloader, validate the file, update the catalog” names activities. It does not say what must remain true if validation fails, which version the consumer should see during replacement, or who may decide that a different resource is an acceptable substitute. Those omissions will become implementation decisions, often without anybody noticing that a decision was made. The handoff from discovery to implementation should preserve the information that constrains those choices. It should also discard conversational material that no longer helps. A transcript may contain abandoned suggestions, tentative interpretations, repeated explanations, and an eventual agreement. Handing all of it to an implementer can obscure which statements now govern the work. For a substantial change, a useful plan is a small current account of the outcome, the decisions that shape it, and the evidence needed to accept it. Supporting investigations remain available by reference. The plan does not need to impersonate the entire repository's documentation. Begin with a consequence the implementer must preserve Our illustrative application already has a usable resource. We want to acquire a replacement, check it, and make it available through the same consumer interface. The central consequence is that a preparation failure before publication must not destroy the working version. This remains an educational example, not a description of Pumas Library's architecture. A compact handoff might read: Outcome: A consumer can open the requested replacement after publication. Until publication succeeds, new consumer requests continue to resolve to the previously active version. Scope: Local acquisition, integrity checking, publication, and status reporting for one supported resource format. Automatic substitution and runtime installation are excluded from this change. Binding decisions: Candidates are prepared outside the active location. Publication changes the active reference only after the selected checks succeed. The publication owner decides whether the transition committed; the progress display cannot make that decision. Unresolved assumption: The supported storage environment must provide the required reference-switch behavior. Investigate this before choosing the publication implementation. Next slice: Establish a consumer-level replacement test and implement the smallest publication path that can satisfy it. Keep acquisition behind a controlled fixture until the publication assumption is resolved. Acceptance: Open the old version while the candidate is held before publication. Reject an invalid candidate and open the old version again. Publish a valid candidate and open the requested replacement. Report the environment and revision exercised. This artifact connects work to behavior. It also changes the order a plausible implementation might otherwise take. Building a sophisticated downloader first would postpone the unresolved assumption that could invalidate the design. The next slice instead investigates the risky publication boundary with a deliberately uninteresting source of bytes. The scope statement is equally consequential. An agent that discovers a missing runtime may report it and propose additional work. It cannot infer permission to install something merely because installation would help the test pass. A plan needs to distinguish an obstacle inside the agreed work from a new product commitment. Preserve reasons selectively Not every decision needs an essay. The reason for staging separately could be one sentence: the current version must remain usable when preparation fails. That sentence helps a later implementer recognize an apparently simpler in-place rewrite as a change in behavior, rather than a harmless refactor. Record a rejected option when its attraction makes it likely to return, or when a new fact could make it preferable. “In-place replacement was rejected because readers could observe partial content” is useful. A catalogue of every library considered during research usually is not. If a lengthy investigation remains relevant, link its conclusion and the conditions under which it should be revisited. Puma's inspected planning standard makes a similar proportional distinction. It permits a clear bounded repair to proceed with an inline write set and acceptance path, while requiring a written plan for material sequencing, contract, migration, coordination, rollout, risk, or acceptance complexity. The rule is an inspectable policy, not evidence that every application of it succeeds. Planning, pinned revision . For a spelling correction in a known status label, the plan might be a sentence. For changing what that label means across a service, API, and interface, the contract must survive several handoffs. The distinction follows the decisions that need preservation, not the number of edited files. Make stale understanding detectable A plan becomes dangerous when it describes a world implementation has already disproved. Suppose inspection reveals that an existing reader holds the active path open throughout its work. The statement about “new consumer requests” remains useful, but the plan now needs to distinguish new readers from existing ones. The implementer should surface that distinction before quietly making old readers follow the replacement too. One current decision owner prevents competing summaries from becoming competing authorities. A task brief can quote the binding rule and link back to it; it should not become an independently editable copy. When the rule changes, affected task owners need the change and its implications, not merely a notification that the document was updated. There is an opposite failure: keeping the plan impeccable while useful work stalls. A discovered alternative can be documented without reopening settled choices that it does not affect. Investigation can also end with the conclusion that no change is needed. A plan is valuable when it helps choose and finish work, including deciding not to start it. Try the handoff without the conversation Choose a real change and give another person, or a fresh agent session, only its compact plan and the referenced repository. Ask for the intended consumer behavior, the first implementation slice, and one condition that requires a new decision. Do not grade whether the answer copies your wording. Check whether it preserves the consequential distinctions. If the recipient can produce a plausible implementation that violates your intention while satisfying every sentence, add the missing invariant or example. If they spend their effort reconciling duplicated guidance, remove a competing copy. The observable outcome is a handoff that permits independent progress while making the next consequential misunderstanding visible.

title: 18 Design the development path
text: 18 Design the development path The order in which software is built affects what can be learned and what can be discarded. A team that integrates three weeks of acquisition work before testing publication has made the publication decision expensive to revisit. A team that creates a branch for every minor step may spend more effort maintaining branch relationships than learning about the product. Both problems begin before the code is wrong. Designing the development path means choosing boundaries where a coherent result becomes inspectable. Sometimes that boundary is a commit. Sometimes it is a disposable experiment, a pull request, or a demonstration against the actual consumer. Git can preserve the boundary, but Git topology cannot supply its purpose. Puma identified branch planning as something to improve. The inspected standards subsequently ask what each development or integration boundary makes visible and what evidence would reopen the design; they explicitly avoid a branch-per-milestone or merge-per-slice rule. That establishes a stated direction, without establishing a measured reduction in revision cost. Development and integration boundaries . Put the earliest useful observation first For the running resource example, the first useful result need not contact a real download service. A controlled candidate can establish whether the consumer sees the old version before publication and the replacement afterward. This makes a risky lifecycle assumption observable with little implementation attached to it. The next boundary can add the real acquisition adapter. Another can expose status through the actual caller. These are vertical observations: each connects a piece of production behavior to something outside that piece. Dividing the work into “all types,” “all services,” and “all interface code” may produce tidy assignments while postponing the first meaningful result until every assignment finishes. A proposed development map could be expressed in ordinary text: Base A: Existing consumer behavior is characterized. Publication slice, A to B: A controlled candidate can replace the active reference; failed preparation leaves the old version usable. One integration owner accepts B. From B, two proposals: The acquisition adapter supplies checked candidates. The interface consumes a fixed status contract. Each proposal names B as its starting contract. Integration C: Exercise the actual caller through acquisition, checking, publication, and failure. Accept the combination only after verifying the shared meaning of completion. The dependency shape is small enough to see at a glance: A: existing behavior | B: publication contract / \ adapter interface \ / C: combined acceptance The letters identify observable development boundaries, not a required Git history. This map has one deliberately serial step. The two later proposals cannot safely work independently until the status and publication contract is understandable. Starting both earlier is possible, but then their work is exploratory and may need revision. Calling the uncertainty “parallelism” does not remove it. Give isolation a job A worktree helps two workers edit without overwriting each other's uncommitted changes. A branch can keep an experiment out of a release candidate. Neither establishes compatibility. The interface branch may interpret completion as “bytes received,” while the acquisition branch means “consumer publication settled.” Their files can merge cleanly and their individual tests can pass. The integration contract therefore belongs beside the branch map. In our example it says that a candidate is not available merely because checking succeeded, and that the active reference changes only at the agreed publication boundary. Both authors can test against this contract before integration. Isolation also needs an ending. A retained branch should have a continuing purpose. A superseded experiment needs a record of what was learned and which commits, if any, remain useful. An abandoned worktree containing the only copy of unfinished work should not disappear during mechanical cleanup. Operational resources and durable explanation have different lifetimes. There is no advantage in manufacturing these obligations for a small serial repair. If one person can make, inspect, and verify a bounded change on the allowed integration path, a separate branch may add no useful isolation. Repository rules can still require one; then the reason is institutional, not an intrinsic property of the change. Keep a serial alternative on the table Mitchell Hashimoto's February 2026 adoption account describes one background coding agent while he continues manual work. He distinguishes that arrangement from parallel research and triage, and avoids assigning work merely to keep agents occupied. The report is a personal workflow, not a comparative trial, but it supplies a serious alternative to a permanent implementation swarm. My AI Adoption Journey . The architectural question is whether extra concurrency shortens the path to an accepted result. Two separable tasks with stable inputs may benefit. Two tasks repeatedly changing the same contract may benefit more from a brief serial decision followed by independent implementation. A worker who finishes quickly but waits a day for integration has improved local throughput without necessarily improving delivery. One useful counterexample is a format-version migration. The parser, writer, and compatibility behavior may be so tightly linked that dividing them between agents creates more assumptions than capacity. A single implementation owner with a separate reviewer can preserve focus while still providing another perspective. Agent count is a resource choice, not a maturity score. Rehearse a change in direction Draw the proposed development path for your next substantial change. At each boundary, write the behavior someone can observe and the fact that would make you reconsider. Then introduce a plausible surprise halfway through: the consumer needs an additional file, publication behaves differently on another platform, or the intended API is unavailable. Identify what survives, what must be redone, and which unintegrated work has become stale. If every discovery forces the whole effort to restart, look for an earlier observation or a smaller commitment. If every boundary exists only because it seemed orderly, combine some. The exercise succeeds when a reviewer can trace a changed assumption to a specific reconsideration point and see the valid work that remains.

title: 19 Give agents bounded responsibilities
text: 19 Give agents bounded responsibilities “Implement acquisition” is a goal with a surprisingly large surface area. An agent might change storage, replace the networking library, alter error handling, add retries, and update the interface. Each action can sound helpful. Together they can outrun the authority and review capacity of the person who delegated the work. A bounded responsibility joins an outcome to a permitted area of action. It gives the worker enough room to solve the assigned problem while identifying choices that belong elsewhere. The boundary must be understandable to the worker and enforceable where enforcement is warranted. A sentence asking the agent to be careful does not isolate its edits or prevent a release. A handoff is a working contract Consider the acquisition adapter after the publication contract has been established. Its handoff could be: Task: Supply a checked candidate to the existing publication interface for the selected local resource. Inputs: The selected identity, source location, expected integrity evidence, the publication contract at the agreed base, and the consumer acceptance examples. Owned changes: The acquisition adapter and its focused tests. Shared status types are read-only until a proposed contract change is accepted by their owner. Required behavior: Acquisition failure leaves the active version unchanged. A retry must not silently select different content. Successful transfer alone must not emit the consumer's available state. Evidence to return: The resulting revision or patch, the focused check results, one failed-acquisition observation, and any assumptions that remain untested. Escalation: Report an unsupported source identity, an inadequate publication contract, or a required change outside the write set. Explain the smallest decision needed and continue independent work where possible. Integration: The integration owner reviews and applies the accepted proposal. The worker does not publish a release. The handoff is short enough to revisit. Its restriction on shared types does not forbid noticing a design problem. It tells the worker how to make that problem visible without silently taking ownership of somebody else's decision. An overly narrow assignment can fail too. “Change only line 42” may force a patch at the symptom when the defect belongs to a different owner. Bounded authority should permit diagnosis and a proposed scope change. It should not reward compliance with an inadequate edit location. Separate four kinds of ownership Task ownership answers who is responsible for reaching a result. Write permission answers what that worker may mutate. Integration ownership answers who combines the work with current authority. Acceptance ownership answers who decides that the result satisfies the intended need. These roles can belong to one person in a small change. They still answer different questions. An implementation agent may own its task while having no authority to approve a change in user-visible behavior. A reviewer may have broad read access while remaining unable to modify the candidate. A release owner may accept a verified change without having written it. The separation becomes useful when work stops unexpectedly. If the caller disconnects, does the task disappear, pause, or continue? Which resources remain held? Where can a replacement worker learn the current status? Tying every answer to the lifetime of one conversation creates avoidable uncertainty. At Passeur revision 71bcac5a , task admission creates a task-owned cancellation controller rather than reusing the caller's signal. The inspected lifecycle tests distinguish a disconnected submitter or cancelled wait from cancellation of the worker. They also check a finite worker-plus-queue capacity. These are concrete source and test assertions; this book's research did not execute them. Task admission , lifecycle tests . That distinction does not imply that every task should continue unattended. The appropriate policy depends on the authority originally granted, the resources in use, and the ability to observe or stop the work. The useful lesson is to make continued execution a deliberate contract rather than a side effect of a lost connection. Make reporting part of useful work A worker should report a finding when it changes a decision, not only when the task is over. Suppose the adapter discovers that the requested resource consists of two files. Waiting until the final report to mention this leaves the interface and tests developing against a false single-file assumption. An early update can be brief: what was found, which assumption it affects, and which work can continue. The opposite failure is a stream of routine narration that consumes the coordinator's attention. Reports should carry information someone can act on: a conflict, a completed usable part, a needed decision, a failed acceptance check, or a material change in scope. The coordinator remains responsible for translating those findings into a coherent account for the requester. A final response of “done” is inadequate when the task contract asked for a patch and evidence. A long explanation without a retrievable result is inadequate too. Return the work in a form that another person can inspect, including failure and uncertainty. Reviewability is a property of the deliverable. Test whether the boundary is real Give a worker the sample handoff and then introduce three situations: an unrelated file needs cleanup, a shared type seems wrong, and the source returns content with an unexpected identity. Ask what the worker would change, report, or refuse to infer. The observable outcome is not a perfect recitation of permissions. It is that the worker can continue useful authorized work, identify the decision owner, and avoid converting convenience into authority. If every surprise blocks the whole task, loosen the boundary around diagnosis. If every surprise justifies broader edits, tighten the distinction between proposing and deciding.

title: 20 Coordinate parallel work while it happens
text: 20 Coordinate parallel work while it happens Two agents can work in different files and still implement incompatible systems. One changes a status producer so that complete means transfer has ended. Another changes a consumer so that complete enables immediate use. No line collides. The combined application announces readiness before publication finishes. This is why coordination cannot be postponed to the merge command. File isolation solves one class of interference. It does not align meanings, preserve decision authority, or discover that two apparently independent tasks rely on the same assumption. Before splitting work, identify the shared promises. For our resource example, these include resource identity, the meaning of availability, the publication boundary, and the survival of the previous version after failure. Workers can own disjoint implementations of those promises. They cannot independently redefine them and expect a clean merge to reconcile the result. Detect the kind of conflict A textual conflict is visible in overlapping edits. A semantic conflict appears when compatible text produces incompatible behavior. An ownership conflict occurs when two workers each believe they may decide the same change. A stale-assumption conflict arises when an otherwise valid proposal depends on a contract that has since changed. These distinctions suggest different responses. Overlapping comments may need a trivial edit. A disagreement about readiness needs a decision and affected tests. A stale proposal may need only revalidation if the intervening change is irrelevant; automatically throwing it away wastes work. Automatically applying it risks restoring an obsolete decision. In the running example, imagine two workers propose changes involving ResourceStatus . The acquisition worker wants to add checked ; the interface worker wants to treat every state other than acquiring as usable. Early coordination could produce this record: Detected dependency: Both proposals depend on the meaning of readiness. Proposal: Add a distinct checked state. Keep usability tied to publication, not to absence of transfer. Acquisition owner: Confirms it can emit the new state without changing publication ownership. Interface owner: Confirms it will remain in a preparing presentation until publication settles; requests a fixture for the held boundary. Integration owner: Accepts the contract revision, updates the shared fixture, and asks both workers to revalidate against that revision before application. Consent here means each affected owner has actually considered the proposed obligation. A coordinator should not write “all agreed” because no worker objected before a deadline. Nor should a worker's agreement be treated as authority to override the requester on a product decision. Guard application where stale state matters Once work has been prepared against a shared base, integration must check whether that base still applies. A proposal can name the contract revision it assumes and the write set it intends. The integrator compares those assumptions to current state before applying it. If they differ, the next step is classification: irrelevant change, compatible adjustment, or a decision that needs reopening. Such a mechanism is useful when several pending proposals can become stale. It may be needless machinery for two read-only researchers and one serial writer. The risk follows mutable shared authority, not participant count. Coordination state itself can become stale. A reservation left by a stopped worker should not block the repository forever, but an old heartbeat does not prove that the owner is gone. A paused process can still own a lock. A new process can reuse a familiar identifier. Recovery is another concurrency problem, with a more dangerous opportunity to mistake uncertainty for permission. Passeur's September 25 repair addresses this at a specific owner. Independent review found a stale-lease recovery race; the implementation introduced a persistent recovery guard and exact-generation checks. Source tests include sixteen competing reclaimers with one successful acquisition, and a paused child that continues to exclude a contender. The recorded checks are bounded Linux/process evidence, not proof of every host recovery path. Repair record , competing reclaimers , paused owner . The application-level lesson is narrower than “add locks.” Mutation authority needs evidence appropriate to the object being protected. The identifier of a task, the generation of a repository lease, and permission to alter a product contract are different kinds of evidence. Ask whether the work should be parallel Coordination has a cost even when it succeeds. Stable independent tasks can amortize that cost. Rapidly changing shared concepts may not. The scaling-agent study provides a useful restraint: its results vary with task structure, and its software evaluations use only twenty tasks in each of two benchmarks. It cannot establish a generally optimal number of coding agents. Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems, version 3 . A practical alternative is to keep one implementation owner and parallelize investigation, test design, or review. Another is to stabilize one small shared contract before opening several write assignments. These choices do not forgo all concurrency. They place it where workers can make progress without repeatedly renegotiating their inputs. Exercise a clean merge that fails Create two small changes in the illustrative application: one changes when the producer emits completion; the other changes when the consumer enables use. Keep their write sets disjoint. Verify that both focused suites can pass while a held-publication integration test fails. Then introduce a shared readiness contract and repeat the handoff. Record when the incompatibility becomes visible and how much work must be revised. Finally, make one proposal stale by changing the contract before application. The observable outcome is early detection plus a justified integration decision, not merely a successful text merge or a larger coordination log.

title: 21 Match models to the work
text: 21 Match models to the work The cheapest model call is not necessarily the cheapest accepted change. A worker can generate a plausible patch quickly, then consume an hour of expert attention repairing its assumptions. A more capable model can spend unnecessary time exploring a task that a short deterministic procedure would have resolved. Choosing between them requires an account of the work, not just a ranking of models. Cost pressure is a reason to evaluate allocation, not evidence that a particular routing policy is already effective. Model capabilities, prices, interfaces, and rate limits change. A durable method should help select the current arrangement without turning today's favorite model into an architectural dependency. Describe the judgment the task requires “Coding” contains several different activities. Locating the source of an error is not the same task as changing a known expression. Comparing two lifecycle designs is not the same as translating a stable interface. Reviewing a concurrency repair requires evidence and skepticism that a broad prose summary may not exercise. For the resource application, consider three assignments: Investigate whether the existing publication operation preserves the old active resource after a failed candidate Implement a bounded acquisition adapter against a stable publication contract Review a candidate for premature completion and resource-lifetime defects The investigation needs relevant retrieval and calibrated uncertainty. The implementation needs reliable local editing and feedback. The review needs the ability to challenge a plausible explanation and construct a counterexample. A model that performs well on one may be poorly suited to another. The surrounding tools and supplied evidence can change the result as much as the model choice. Some tasks should not be routed to open-ended judgment at all. A known formatting transformation or schema validation may already have a reliable tool. An agent can invoke it without being asked to reinvent its rules. Build a small evaluation around acceptance A useful first evaluation can be modest. Select several representative, already understood tasks from each class. Keep their desired outcomes and environments stable. Give each candidate the inputs it would receive in actual work. Save the model version, relevant settings, tool access, and supplied context so that a later result is interpretable. The evaluation record might contain: Task family: Bounded adapters for local resources. Required result: The requested resource is acquired and checked; failed preparation preserves the active version; no unauthorized contract expansion occurs. Candidate arrangements: One model with the existing tools; another with the same tools; a prescribed localization-and-edit procedure using a model only at designated steps. Observations: Accepted or rejected result, reason for rejection, elapsed time, human intervention time, tool and inference cost, retries, and integration repairs. Hard constraints: No unapproved dependencies, no changes outside the task's authority, and no acceptance based solely on the worker's report. Decision: Prefer the least costly arrangement that meets the required quality and risk constraints for this task family; retain an escalation path for cases outside the tested range. This is a proposed experiment, not a table of measured results. Its most important property is that all candidates must earn the same kind of acceptance. A cheap candidate should not receive easier tests, while an expensive one is charged for more demanding scrutiny. The simpler arrangement deserves genuine consideration. Agentless studied a prescribed localization, repair, and validation pipeline and obtained competitive results on its historical benchmark without an open-ended agent workflow. It still used language models. Its relevance here is the existence of a credible procedural baseline, not a claim that interactive agents are unnecessary for current development. Agentless, version 2 . Count the expensive parts you can overlook Inference spend is observable and easy to compare, which makes it tempting to treat it as the whole bill. Include repeated context, tool execution, test environments, unsuccessful attempts, merge repair, and human attention. Report elapsed delivery time separately: a background task can take longer on the clock while requiring less active supervision. Avoid collapsing everything into one monetary number unless the conversions serve an actual decision. Ten minutes of scarce maintainer attention may matter more than a small cloud charge, but assigning an invented hourly value can hide that fact behind false precision. A small set of dimensions is often more honest: accepted quality, human minutes, elapsed time, and direct cost. Sample size limits what the evaluation can settle. One success is a useful demonstration. It is weak evidence for routine reliability. One unusually difficult task can also distort a tiny comparison. Inspect failure patterns, repeat material cases when feasible, and report how much of the real workload the sample represents. The evaluation can reveal that task design is the bottleneck. If every model misunderstands whether checking implies availability, routing among them may have little value until the contract is repaired. Likewise, if every candidate spends most of its time waiting for a build, a faster model may not shorten delivery. Use escalation without surrendering authority A practical routing policy can start bounded tasks with a less expensive arrangement and escalate on named signals: repeated failure at the same boundary, unresolved architectural uncertainty, or an inability to produce trustworthy evidence. Escalation should carry the current state and failed approaches, not ask a new model to reconstruct everything from a triumphant summary. Changing models does not grant new permissions. A stronger reviewer is still a reviewer; a stronger implementer still owns the same task. Nor does provider diversity establish independent reasoning. Models can share missing context, common patterns, and the same mistaken oracle. Test one allocation decision Choose a task family you actually repeat. Compare two arrangements on a small set of representative cases and include at least one unsuccessful attempt in the record. Ask a reviewer who did not generate the patches to apply the same acceptance criteria. The observable outcome is a bounded rule such as “use arrangement A for these stable adapters, escalate when publication semantics change,” with the evidence and uncertainty attached. If the sample cannot distinguish the candidates, say so. An inconclusive comparison is more useful than a permanent model hierarchy built from impression.

title: 22 Revise the plan without losing the goal
text: 22 Revise the plan without losing the goal Implementation is an encounter with facts the plan could not fully contain. The resource has an auxiliary file nobody mentioned. A filesystem operation behaves differently under the supported deployment. A consumer needs metadata before it can open otherwise valid bytes. Finding one of these conditions is not itself a planning failure. The failure is to conceal the discovery, or to treat every discovery as permission to redefine the outcome. The plan should be revisable because the goal matters. Its current form is a means of preserving decisions while work proceeds. Once an assumption becomes false, faithful execution can become a way of building the wrong thing more efficiently. Classify the new fact before changing the work Suppose the acquisition adapter now obtains both the main resource and an auxiliary file. The existing progress calculation uses the known size of the main resource as its total, while received bytes include both files. There are several possible questions here, and they should not be bundled into one vague request to “fix progress.” The known total may be a false measurement assumption. The meaning of completion may be an inadequate contract. The presentation of unknown progress may be an unresolved product choice. A proposal to substitute a different resource is a change of scope. Each belongs to a different decision, even if one test first exposes all of them. For our illustrative application, assume the main requirement remains: a valid selected replacement becomes usable, while the old version survives a preparation failure before publication. Discovering an auxiliary file does not automatically change that goal. It changes what acquisition must include and what can truthfully be reported during preparation. A revision record could say: Observation: The selected resource includes a required auxiliary file whose size is unavailable before transfer. Invalidated assumption: The known main-file size represents total acquisition size. Preserved decisions: Selection identity remains fixed. Publication waits for all required checking. The active version survives failure before publication. An uncertain publication result requires reconciliation, not an assumed rollback. Changed contract: Total size and estimated remaining time may be unknown. Availability continues to depend on publication, independent of any displayed fraction. Affected work: Acquisition accounting, status serialization, interface presentation, and tests that assume a known denominator. Decision needed: Select how the interface communicates ongoing work when the total is unknown. The measurement must remain unknown regardless of the presentation choice. This record makes it possible to keep valid implementation. It also prevents a convenient percentage from becoming permission to invent a total. Propagate consequences, not just text Updating the plan is the beginning of a revision. Each affected worker needs to know which assumption changed and whether its current proposal remains valid. Tests may need a new fixture. An API example may need to represent absence. A previously reviewed diff may now require another look at the changed contract. The integration owner should classify work rather than resetting everything. An adapter that already carries an optional total may remain usable. A presentation that divides by the total without checking absence does not. A publication test can remain valid if it never depended on progress arithmetic. This selective approach reduces rework without pretending the change has no consequences. Keep the history of the previous decision intelligible. A future maintainer should be able to tell that a number was removed because its evidence was inadequate, not because somebody forgot to calculate it. The current plan should contain the current rule; a short dated record can preserve why it changed. Two competing active versions create uncertainty rather than traceability. Sometimes the rule is what needs repair It is tempting to respond to every failure by adding a stricter gate. A gate can also be based on the wrong ownership model. Passeur's October 1 record describes a Muse task whose native work produced a commit but was classified as interrupted because ordinary SDK startup lacked a protected-launcher stop proof. The repair made successful SDK close the ordinary requirement and demanded additional proof only when that launcher owned it. Recorded focused checks passed, while broader failures remained unqualified. This was a correction to an evidence contract, not permission to assume shutdown. Operational report , adapter repair . The important question is whether a requirement protects a real obligation at the correct owner. “More checks” does not answer it. A rule can reject valid work, obscure responsibility, or make the system impossible to operate without improving the outcome it was meant to protect. Steve Yegge's September 2026 Wheelhouse account offers a larger, explicitly personal example: he describes accumulated constraints stopping progress and a substantial reduction in refusal sites. The account also discusses spending and task-sizing pressures. These are operator reports rather than controlled findings, but they challenge the assumption that adding orchestration rules is a one-way improvement. Seats and Sunsets . Removing an unnecessary rule still requires understanding its purpose. Deleting a failing acceptance test solely to obtain a green run erases the question the test was asking. Revising a test because it encoded a disproved assumption can be correct, provided the intended outcome is checked by a better observation. Decide when to involve the requester An implementer can often correct an internal assumption within the granted scope. A change to the promised behavior, supported audience, cost, privacy, or release commitment belongs with the person authorized to decide it. The useful escalation explains the consequence and offers a bounded choice. It does not ask the requester to resolve an implementation detail that the developer already understands. If the requester cannot decide immediately, preserve the working version and continue independent work. Do not use silence as acceptance of a broadened objective. Equally, do not freeze unrelated tasks whose inputs remain valid. Rehearse an amendment Take the plan from chapter 17 and add the unknown-size auxiliary file. Identify every assumption that changes, then mark each pending task as unaffected, needing adjustment, or blocked on a decision. Rewrite one acceptance example before changing implementation. The exercise succeeds when another reader can explain both what changed and what still governs the work. They should also be able to identify who decides the unresolved presentation choice. A revised plan that merely matches the current code has not yet demonstrated that it preserves the goal.

title: 23 Test the outcome as well as implementation
text: Part 5 Establish that the result deserves trust Completion requires a bounded account of what was observed and what remains unknown. Tests, review, failure experiments, and measurements answer different questions; the following chapters explain how they can support a useful acceptance decision. 23 Test the outcome as well as implementation The download test passes. The expected bytes exist. The checksum matches. A user selects the resource and receives “not available.” Every preceding observation can be true. The missing link is between what the implementation checked and what the user was promised. Testing an outcome begins with the action that should become possible. In the running example, a consumer must open the selected replacement through the supported interface after publication. Before that boundary, the old version must remain usable. A test that inspects only a staging directory cannot establish either claim. This does not make lower-level tests unimportant. They locate defects and exercise cases that would be expensive through the whole application. The challenge is to build an evidence chain whose links answer different questions, rather than accumulate many assertions about the same intermediate event. Name the oracle A test oracle is the basis for deciding whether an observed result is correct. Sometimes it is a simple expected value. Sometimes it is a domain invariant, a known implementation, or a person's judgment about behavior. Whatever its form, it can be wrong. For acquisition, “the returned status equals complete ” is a weak oracle if the implementation itself decides when to return that status. A stronger acceptance observation asks the real consumer to open the requested identity and checks the content or behavior it receives. The status can then be checked against that independent consequence. Independence is practical rather than absolute. The consumer might share the same faulty catalog code. A checksum might come from the same untrusted source as the bytes. A second implementation might preserve a defect in the first. State what each oracle depends on, especially where agreement could reflect a shared mistake. Test both sides of a boundary A useful publication test is a sequence, not just an eventual success assertion. In the illustrative application: Install a known old version and prove the consumer can use it Begin preparing a valid replacement, then hold execution immediately before publication Confirm that a new consumer request still resolves to the old version and that status does not claim the replacement is available Release publication and confirm that a new request resolves to the selected replacement Repeat with an invalid candidate and confirm that the old version remains usable after the failure The controlled hold makes a normally short interval observable. Without it, a fast machine may race past the defect so that a polling test never sees it. The barrier must be released during teardown even when an assertion fails; otherwise the test can strand the worker it was meant to inspect. Pumas provides a bounded real counterpart. At draft head 42a198bf , a public HF status test holds the importer at a metadata-write barrier. The input files already exist, but the test requires nonterminal status and no completion receipt. After release, it checks completion alongside the receipt, model/index presence, adopted acquisition state, and queue release. The repository reports a focused pass; the test was not rerun for this book. It exercises a controlled Linux public-core/DTO path, not JSON-RPC, Electron, or every supported platform. Public-boundary test , recorded execution and limits . The transferable technique is to make the consequential interval testable and inspect what consumers can observe there. The particular internal state names belong to that repository. Include the actual entry point A function-level test can establish a sound core while a wrapper mishandles units, errors, or completion. At least one acceptance path should therefore use the interface the relevant consumer actually calls. For a command-line tool, invoke the command. For an API, exercise the protocol boundary. For a desktop interaction, inspect the interface and its behavior under the intended conditions. Simon Willison's account of agentic manual testing advocates this complementary practice: start the system, invoke its interfaces, inspect observed output, and convert useful discoveries into regressions. His Showboat approach records commands and output rather than relying only on an agent's narrative. Such a demonstration covers the behavior exercised; it is not a proof of unvisited paths. Agentic manual testing . Exploration and repeatable tests serve different purposes. Exploration can reveal a confusing status transition nobody thought to specify. A regression can make that discovered requirement durable. Automating every exploratory observation immediately may be wasteful; leaving a consequential repeated failure dependent on memory is wasteful in another way. Make a passing suite vulnerable to a meaningful fault Ask what deliberate defect should cause the suite to fail. Move the availability signal before publication. Replace the requested identity with a different valid resource. Delete the old active version before checking the candidate. If a suite still passes, it does not establish the corresponding claim, however large its test count. This is a useful local mutation exercise, not a demand to construct an exhaustive mutation-testing framework. Choose a fault tied to a material promise. The result often exposes that several tests copied the implementation's assumptions rather than checking an external consequence. Acceptance can also require human observation. A technically accurate progress display might be misleading because the user reasonably interprets a finished bar as permission to close the application. Describe that interpretation and inspect the actual flow. Human judgment should address the unresolved experience, not replace checks that the machine can perform precisely. Build one complete evidence chain Take a change whose tests already pass. Write the promised consumer action, the observation that proves it became possible, and one plausible defect the current tests could miss. Add or perform the smallest check that distinguishes the defect from the desired behavior. Record the exercised revision and environment, then state one important limit. The observable outcome is an acceptance claim supported by a relevant observation, including a failure case. A larger passing count is optional; a clearer connection to the intended result is the point.

title: 24 Use independent review effectively
text: 24 Use independent review effectively A second agent reads a patch and agrees with the first. This may be useful, but the number two does not establish independence. Both agents may have received the same mistaken requirement, trusted the same passing test, and followed the same persuasive explanation. Two approvals can therefore be two presentations of one blind spot. Effective review creates an opportunity to challenge the work from a different position. The reviewer needs enough context to understand the promise, enough access to inspect the result, and enough freedom to disagree with the implementer's account. The goal is a justified acceptance decision, not a ritual exchange of approval. Give the reviewer a question worth answering “Review this for bugs” can be a useful broad request, but it should not be the only instruction for a consequential boundary. For the acquisition change, ask whether failed replacement preserves the usable old version, whether completion corresponds to consumer availability, and whether cancellation can release resources still in use. Supply the exact candidate revision, the intended behavior, the diff, relevant contracts, and reproducible evidence. Include known failures and unrun checks. Let the reviewer inspect the implementer's rationale, but do not make agreement with it the assignment. A reviewer who cannot verify a claim should be able to report that limitation without inventing a defect. A bounded review brief could read: Review candidate R against base B for the replacement lifecycle. Focus on publication ordering, old-version survival, and cancellation while blocking work remains active. Inspect production paths and the tests that claim to cover them. Do not modify the candidate. Return actionable findings, material uncertainty, and the scope you actually inspected. A clean report applies only to R and that scope. The read-only role makes it easier to separate findings from repairs. If the reviewer silently fixes the code, the author may never understand the defect, and the reviewed revision becomes ambiguous. A reviewer can propose a repair or be given a subsequent implementation task; the transition should be explicit. Require a finding to carry its consequence Consider an illustrative finding: Behavior: Cancelling the public waiter releases the candidate directory while a blocking checker can still read it. Location: The boundary that starts the checker retains the task handle but does not retain the directory's ownership capability. Consequence: A replacement attempt can acquire the same directory before the first checker finishes. Counterexample: Hold the checker, cancel the waiter, and try the competing acquisition. It must remain excluded until the checker returns. Uncertainty: This follows from the inspected lifetime path; the competing acquisition has not yet been exercised on the target platform. This report is useful even before a patch exists. It names the violated promise, the mechanism, a distinguishing observation, and its present evidential limit. “Race condition, high severity” without those details can consume more attention than it saves. Severity should follow consequence and reachability, not dramatic terminology. A race in an unreachable fixture differs from a race at a public cancellation boundary. A style disagreement can be valuable without being a release blocker. The reviewer should distinguish a demonstrated defect, a plausible risk requiring investigation, and a preferred alternative. Allocate human understanding deliberately Practitioners disagree about how much source a human must read. That disagreement deserves more than a compromise slogan. Simon Willison argues that unreviewed generated patches can transfer the real work to collaborators; his proposed contribution standard includes a small understood change and evidence of testing. This is a responsibility norm rather than a measured defect-detection rate. Anti-patterns . Salvatore Sanfilippo's July 2026 essay places more emphasis on controlling design ideas, comparative checks, performance, and QA than on routinely reading every generated line. He still describes reading Redis code for its maintainers and users, and leaves some skill-development questions open. His position challenges universal line-review requirements without removing the need to understand the system. Control the ideas, not the code . Daniel Stenberg describes AI review after human review while retaining human architectural and merge responsibility for curl. That is a different allocation suited to a long-lived shared system, not proof that a particular sequence always finds more defects. A human in control . The decision should reflect what must be understood and who will maintain the result. In a disposable personal experiment, behavior-focused QA may be sufficient. In a shared parser that handles hostile input, accepting a large generated change without a maintainer able to reason about its structure may be unacceptable. These settings do not differ merely in how enthusiastic their authors are about AI. Design review, source review, runtime testing, and differential comparison reveal different failure classes. One cannot be substituted for another solely because it is easier to automate. Conversely, requiring every method on every tiny change can make review too costly to perform well. Close findings against the repaired revision Once the author changes the candidate, verify that the repair addresses the counterexample and preserves neighboring behavior. A passing new test is useful, but inspect whether the test actually reaches the former defect. Review the incremental repair instead of repeatedly regenerating the whole implementation and forcing everyone to start again. The final acceptance record should name which findings were fixed, rejected with reasons, or deferred under an explicit decision. A later unrelated commit does not inherit an unlimited clean bill of health. Nor must a bounded review expand forever into every architectural concern a reviewer can imagine. For an exercise, give a reviewer the chapter 23 acceptance claim and a candidate with premature completion deliberately introduced. Withhold your proposed diagnosis. Ask for a counterexample and a scope-limited conclusion. Repair the defect, then ask the reviewer to check the new revision. The observable result is a traceable finding-to-repair-to-verification sequence, including any claim the reviewer could not establish.

title: 25 Design for interruption and failure
text: 25 Design for interruption and failure An operation is easiest to explain when every step returns. The interesting questions begin when a process disappears after changing state but before reporting the result. Did publication fail, or did the acknowledgment fail? Is the worker gone, or has only its caller stopped waiting? Can cleanup proceed, or is some effect still using the files? These are not exceptional questions appended to a completed design. They determine ownership and observable behavior. If the application promises that an unsuccessful replacement preserves the working version, that promise must survive the interruption points the application claims to handle. The running example has three broad phases: acquire a candidate, check it, and publish it. That description is enough to start identifying failures, but it is not enough to decide recovery. We also need to know which state is authoritative, which effects can continue independently, and how a later observer distinguishes a completed action from an unattempted one. Stop treating cancellation as one event Cancellation can mean that a caller no longer wants a result, that a worker has been asked to stop, that the worker has actually stopped, or that cleanup has finished. Those events can occur at different times. Collapsing them into one boolean invites a resource to be reused while an old effect can still access it. For example, a blocking checker may outlive the async task waiting for it. Cancelling the waiter does not necessarily terminate the checker. The ownership capability must remain with work that can still use the candidate, and shutdown must account for that work. A timeout provides an observation about waiting; it does not prove cessation. Passeur's inspected transport distinguishes parent-process exit from stream closure because a descendant can retain the output stream. A controlled native fixture leaves such a descendant alive and expects close to remain unconfirmed. This establishes a specific process boundary in source and test assertions, not a guarantee for every provider's process tree. Transport observation , descendant fixture . If stop is uncertain, the system needs an explicit unresolved state and a recovery path. Starting a replacement worker immediately may duplicate effects. Waiting forever without exposing the obligation is also a failure of operability. The appropriate response can be to block conflicting mutation, retain evidence, and request the observation or decision that resolves ownership. Put failure points beside the intended guarantees A small fault plan for the illustrative acquisition can be written as four cases: During acquisition: Interrupt before the candidate is complete. The active reference must still open the old version. Partial candidate bytes must remain either owned for a defined recovery path or eligible for safe cleanup. During checking: Hold a checker, request cancellation, and attempt conflicting reuse. Reuse must remain excluded while the checker can access the candidate. At publication: Interrupt after the authoritative state might have changed but before the caller receives its result. Recovery must inspect that state and identify the exact candidate; a missing acknowledgment alone cannot justify another publication. After publication: Interrupt before cleanup or status notification. The published resource must remain usable, and recovery must not remove it while treating the incomplete notification as a failed candidate. The third case exposes an important qualification to “failure preserves the old version.” A reported error does not prove the publication itself failed. If publication committed, recovery must describe that outcome truthfully. Keeping the previous version available for deliberate rollback can be useful, but silently rolling back on every communication error introduces another state change that also needs authority and evidence. Retries need the same care. Retrying the same intended acquisition should retain its identity. Starting a new acquisition that happens to use the same URL may select different content if the source is mutable. A retry policy cannot repair an unspecified identity contract. Match the claim to the fault actually exercised Pumas's draft acquisition work includes a Linux subprocess test that kills a child after native destination rename and directory synchronization, before metadata publication. The test then checks exact receipt-based recovery without new requests to its controlled source. This is useful evidence about one SIGKILL boundary. It does not reproduce sudden power loss, establish other filesystems' durability, or qualify Windows and macOS. The book's research inspected the test and repository reports rather than rerunning it. Crash-boundary regression . That limitation is part of the engineering result. Different faults invalidate different assumptions. Throwing an exception preserves the process and much of its memory. Killing a process removes that memory but leaves the operating system alive. Losing power challenges persistence below the process. A network partition creates uncertainty at more than one observer. A claim should name the fault class, environment, and boundary tested. Failure injection should also be safe for the test environment. Use disposable roots, controlled sources, bounded cleanup, and a way to release held workers when assertions fail. A test that corrupts unrelated data or strands a process has introduced a new lifecycle problem. Give long-running development its own recovery design The same reasoning applies to the agent doing the work. Save a useful candidate, current assumptions, failed checks, and the next bounded action where another session can inspect them. A long conversation is not a durable result by itself. Armin Ronacher's September 2026 account describes an intentionally oversized, largely unattended CPython experiment that ran for about 35 hours and produced extensive code and commits without an outcome he considered useful. He acknowledges the setup's limitations. The episode is a counterexample to equating continued activity with progress, not evidence that all long-running agent work fails. Astra for Coding . A stop condition should concern the ability to continue usefully: repeated attempts without new evidence, a missing decision, exhausted authorized resources, or an acceptance requirement that the environment cannot exercise. Stopping should preserve the result and explain the blocker. It should not pretend an unfinished task is complete merely because a turn ended. Interrupt one boundary deliberately Choose one phase transition in your application and state what must remain true on both sides. Add a controlled interruption, attempt the forbidden competing action, then recover through the public owner. Record the exact environment and fault class. The observable outcome is a state you can explain after interruption, with resource ownership intact and no invented success. If you cannot tell whether publication occurred, preserve that uncertainty and improve the recovery observation before adding automatic retry.

title: 26 Measure before optimizing
text: 26 Measure before optimizing An agent notices that the test suite repeatedly constructs a temporary repository. It proposes sharing a fixture. That may be an excellent optimization. It may also allow one test's mutations to affect another, or save little time because compilation dominates the run. The first task is to discover which situation applies. Optimization begins with a desired consequence. “Fewer subprocesses” is a mechanism. “A developer gets reliable feedback soon enough to stay in the task” is an outcome. Intermediate measures can explain the outcome, but they should not quietly replace it. The same applies to agent workflows. Fewer tokens can mean less irrelevant context or less necessary information. More parallel workers can reduce waiting or increase integration repair. A faster first patch can still take longer to accept. Measurement should follow the result the team actually values. Establish the unit of comparison Consider an illustrative investigation of a slow standards-engine test suite. The hypothesis is that repeated fixture construction, rather than the assertions themselves, dominates execution. No performance result is asserted here; this is a worked measurement design. An investigation record could be: Outcome: Reduce the time to reliable suite feedback without changing what the suite checks or introducing order dependence. Baseline: Record the exact revision, test selection, command, machine, process settings, and cache conditions. Separate setup time, test-body time, and teardown where feasible. Hypothesis: Repeated construction of an equivalent immutable corpus accounts for enough of the run to justify reuse. Candidate change: Reuse only the immutable source fixture. Give each mutating test its own derived state. Comparison: Run the same workload before and after under comparable conditions. Include repeated runs, changed test order where relevant, and checks that a mutation cannot leak between tests. Decision: Retain the optimization only if the observed improvement matters and the isolation contract remains credible. The record prevents an easy mistake: changing both the fixture and the test workload, then attributing the whole difference to reuse. It also keeps correctness in view. A fast suite that occasionally inherits a previous test's state is worse feedback, even if its median runtime improves. Measure enough to answer the decision. A small isolated optimization may need simple timings and a clear distribution of observed variation. A noisy shared runner may require more repetitions or a more controlled comparison. Sophisticated statistics cannot rescue a workload that does not represent the actual use. Interpret intermediate measures carefully Suppose instrumentation confirms that the candidate launches fewer processes. That supports a mechanism claim. It does not yet establish shorter end-to-end execution, lower memory use, or faster development. Those are separate observations. Likewise, a smaller agent-tool catalog can reduce payload bytes while increasing discovery calls. A narrower task can reduce context while shifting specification work to the coordinator. These tradeoffs may be worthwhile. They need to be counted where they occur. For the running resource application, total acquisition latency can be decomposed into locating the source, transferring bytes, checking, publishing, and making the result visible to the consumer. If checking dominates a particular workload, improving connection setup may not change the experience materially. If publication blocks all readers, average transfer speed may be the wrong priority altogether. Use representative sizes and failure cases. A tiny cached fixture may hide the path that matters. An enormous synthetic input may exaggerate a bottleneck absent from normal use. Report what the workload represents and what it excludes. Measure development without confusing its clocks Active human time, elapsed delivery time, and machine cost are different quantities. A background agent can require little attention while taking hours. Several simultaneous tasks can overlap elapsed time while competing for the same review capacity. Summing their wall-clock durations does not yield the person's working time. METR's early-2025 randomized study found a slowdown for experienced contributors using the evaluated tools on familiar mature repositories. That is a result in a particular population and period, not a permanent verdict on coding assistance. Its 2026 continuation warns that selection effects and measuring concurrent-agent work make newer estimates unreliable. The useful response is careful local measurement, not choosing whichever headline confirms an existing preference. Early-2025 trial , 2026 update . A local comparison should include specification, supervision, unsuccessful attempts, review, repair, and integration. Keep quality criteria stable. If one workflow produces more ambitious results, record that change in scope rather than calling the longer duration a simple slowdown or the extra output a simple speedup. Subjective experience matters too. A developer may find a workflow less tiring or more enjoyable without finishing faster. That can be valuable, but it is a different claim. Record it in its own terms rather than forcing it into a productivity number. Look for the receiving bottleneck Daniel Stenberg's April 2026 curl account describes a shift from low-quality report overload toward useful findings arriving faster than the project could comfortably remediate and distribute fixes. The changing report mix and operating conditions prevent a simple causal attribution to AI. The maintenance lesson is nevertheless concrete: better discovery can move the limiting work downstream. High-Quality Chaos . For agent-assisted development, the receiver may be the reviewer, integrator, release engineer, or user who must evaluate changed behavior. Improving generation without considering that receiver can enlarge a queue of plausible unfinished work. A useful optimization may therefore reduce batch size or improve evidence rather than increase patch output. Once the relevant checks pass and the decision is supported, stop measuring for this change. More instrumentation has its own maintenance cost. Keep enough evidence to understand the result and revisit it when the workload or environment materially changes. Test one suspected bottleneck Choose a delay you routinely notice. State its consequence, measure the baseline, and identify one change that could affect it. Hold the workload and acceptance criteria steady while comparing the candidate. Include an unsuccessful or noisy observation rather than retaining only the best run. The exercise succeeds when you can say what improved, by how much under the observed conditions, and what did not follow from the measurement. Discovering that the suspected bottleneck is unimportant is a useful result: it prevents a confident optimization of the wrong thing.

title: 27 Finish with evidence
text: 27 Finish with evidence A change can be implemented, tested locally, reviewed, integrated, and still not accepted for its intended use. These are distinct states because they answer distinct questions. Treating them all as “done” forces the next person to reconstruct what actually happened. Completion should be a bounded claim about a particular result. It identifies what was requested, what revision carries the result, which observations support it, and which obligations remain. This is neither a victory speech nor an archive of every command. It is the account someone needs to decide what they can safely rely on next. The resource example gives us a concrete target. The change is complete for its agreed scope when the selected replacement can be used after publication, failed preparation preserves the working version, and the required evidence supports that behavior in the named environment. A future desire for another source provider does not automatically keep this change open. A required publication check that never ran does. Bind the claim to the candidate A passing result belongs to the revision and environment exercised. Subsequent source changes may invalidate it. A documentation-only successor can sometimes preserve the relevant implementation evidence, but that relationship should be justified rather than assumed.
