A report copied from an earlier branch is historical evidence, not a fresh run. The inspected Coding-Standards history provides an uncomfortable and useful example. At main revision dcc56f26 , the exact-head hosted Engine job reported 613 tests with one failure. The failing proposal-analysis test received AUTHORING.INVALID_SEMANTIC_REVISION ; the later complete verification command was not reached because the shell stopped on failure. Passing earlier groups did not make the whole gate pass. Observed hosted job , workflow sequence . Source inspection showed a fixture hardcoding accepted revision one for a policy whose current declaration was revision two. That strongly supports a stale-fixture diagnosis. It does not show that a repair was applied or that the intended projection-count assertion passed afterward. The book's research made no repair and performed no rerun. Fixture , current declaration . The distinction is practical. “The failure appears to be an obsolete fixture” tells a maintainer what to investigate. “Verification passed” would tell them something the evidence does not establish. A persuasive diagnosis cannot stand in for the missing observation. Write an account someone can use For the illustrative application, a release account awaiting a required hosted check might read: Result: Candidate R1 implements replacement through the supported local consumer. Preparation failures preserve the old active version. No additional source provider or runtime installation is included. Local evidence: The recorded checks cover opening the old version before publication, rejecting an invalid candidate, opening the requested replacement after publication, and cancellation while checking is held. The record names the commands, environment, and candidate R1. Review: The lifecycle reviewer inspected R0 and found premature completion. The repair produced R1; the reviewer rechecked the finding on R1, and the local checks above exercised R1. Any later source change requires assessment of which evidence remains applicable. Integration: R1 is on the agreed integration branch. The required hosted verification of R1 has failed, so release acceptance remains blocked. Next obligation: Investigate the failing hosted check, repair within the agreed scope, and obtain the missing result. The release owner makes the acceptance decision after that evidence is available. This is a specimen of wording, not a report of tests performed on a real application. It demonstrates that substantial useful work can be complete while a specific release obligation remains open. The account gives the next worker a concrete continuation rather than either an exaggerated success or a vague “not done.” When all required checks pass, the account can become shorter. State the delivered behavior, revision, verification, material limits, and destination. Do not make the user navigate a long ledger to find the answer to whether they can use the result. Keep unknowns distinct from defects An untested platform is not automatically a known failure. A failed required check is not merely an untested platform. A known defect accepted for a bounded release is different from either, and should name who accepted the consequence and under what conditions. This distinction prevents both overclaiming and needless paralysis. If the agreed release supports one local platform, absence of qualification elsewhere can be an explicit limit. If cross-platform behavior is part of the promise, the same absence is a blocker. Acceptance follows the intended scope rather than a universal checklist. Do not hide unresolved incidents behind nearby successful repairs. A source defect may have been corrected without reproducing the original report. Preserve the distinction until the evidence connects them. Likewise, an operator's decision to retire an uncertain task does not rewrite its historical outcome into confirmed success. Finish the operational edges Delivery includes the artifacts someone needs to use or continue the work: the actual patch or release, the relevant documentation, and retrievable evidence. Temporary branches and environments should receive a justified disposition. Cleanup must preserve uniquely held work and any evidence required for recovery or maintenance. Remaining tasks should have a purpose and an owner. “Improve everything later” is not a useful obligation. “Qualify the same publication behavior on the second supported platform before enabling it there” is. If a required external process is still running, completion reporting should reflect that and the responsible person should continue following it to a result. There is also a stopping rule. Once the requested outcome is accepted and its operational obligations are resolved, unrelated architectural ambitions belong to another decision. A rigorous process should make completion easier to recognize, not place it beyond reach. Audit the word done Take a recently completed change and try to reconstruct its claim from the final report alone. Can you identify the exact candidate, the behavior delivered, the checks that ran, the checks that failed or did not run, the review scope, and the acceptance decision? Rewrite the account so another person can distinguish evidence from diagnosis and current status from historical success. The observable outcome is a reader who knows what they may rely on and what, if anything, still needs action. That is a useful end to a change and a trustworthy beginning for the next one.

title: 28 Grow shared foundations from demonstrated needs
text: Part 6 Build an ecosystem without losing the products The final part examines the broader consequences of the approach: shared foundations, usable releases, representations beyond source text, and the process’s own need to remain open to criticism and revision. 28 Grow shared foundations from demonstrated needs An ecosystem begins to make sense when several products need the same responsibility handled well. It becomes difficult to direct when every possible future use is treated as a present requirement. Several systems may encounter recurring needs: model management, execution, agent composition, coordination, knowledge representation, and provenance. Those connections justify investigating shared infrastructure. They do not establish that the systems should become one monolith or that proposed integrations already work. A shared foundation should have a reason that can be expressed through actual consumers. Draw responsibilities before dependencies A repository diagram often begins with arrows. An arrow is ambiguous. It may mean a runtime dependency, a shared concept, a planned integration, a source of research, or merely an application that might benefit later. First describe the responsibility: managing resources, executing work, composing agents, preserving records, supplying guidance, or coordinating participants. An application may need several of these responsibilities without sharing the same purpose or information model as another application. Then label the connection. Is there an inspected call path? A shared data contract? A proposal to adapt an idea? A dependency needed for an end-to-end release? The label prevents architectural intention from becoming a false implementation claim. A responsibility map describes a proposed architecture. Concrete implementation claims need evidence from observed call paths, contracts, and behavior; a connection on a diagram is not that evidence. Extract the common rule rather than the first application's schema Suppose two applications need durable records. They may share transaction handling, identity, ordering, and retention mechanisms. They may not share the meaning of a workflow result, a research claim, or a model-loading attempt. If the common layer encodes the first application's tables as its public domain, the second application must imitate that application's assumptions. The extraction has preserved code while missing the common responsibility. A better investigation asks which invariants genuinely match. Can both applications use the same record identity and append semantics? Do they need the same consistency boundary? Which fields belong to the application and should remain opaque to the storage mechanism? The result might be a small shared component rather than a broad platform. That is a legitimate foundation if it removes a demonstrated duplication without centralizing unrelated meaning. Give a shared layer its own product contract Infrastructure is used by people and agents. It needs discoverable capabilities, understandable failures, versioning, and a definition of supported behavior. Treating it as an internal convenience can leave callers dependent on incidental structure. A shared layer also creates an organizational obligation. Who accepts a change that benefits one consumer but burdens another? How are incompatible requirements represented? Who owns migration? These questions matter even when one person currently maintains all the repositories, because agents can act as separate consumers with different local contexts. An abstraction should make disagreement explicit. If one consumer needs durable retention and another needs ephemeral cleanup, do not bury the difference in a boolean whose meaning changes by caller. Establish the policy boundary and show what each choice costs. Keep independent projects independent where it helps A project can contribute ideas without becoming a runtime dependency. A ledger or workflow experiment may inform another system while remaining useful on its own. Knowledge-graph work may reveal needs relevant to research or memory tools without imposing one application schema everywhere. This independence can improve learning: a concept encounters a different problem and reveals which assumptions were local. It can also produce duplicated effort. The decision should be based on the value of those different contexts, not a reflex to consolidate everything. For an exercise, draw a map of three projects using five connection labels: implemented dependency, shared contract, planned integration, research influence, and product prerequisite. Select one shared foundation and identify two actual consumer scenarios. If their invariants do not match, narrow the proposed common layer. The map is useful when it prevents an unnecessary dependency or clarifies a real one.

title: 29 Balance foundational work with usable releases
text: 29 Balance foundational work with usable releases A foundation can be necessary and still become a reason that no product reaches a user. Each layer exposes another problem worth solving. Model handling leads to runtime management. Runtime management leads to acquisition and resource ownership. Execution leads to scheduling. Scheduling leads to distributed coordination. The work can remain technically meaningful while the original application stays out of reach. Define the smallest valuable end-to-end result A horizontal milestone completes a layer: the registry, the scheduler, the ledger. A vertical milestone lets a person do something useful through the necessary layers. For our running example, a vertical result could be selecting one supported resource, acquiring it, verifying readiness, and using it from a real consumer. It may support only a narrow model and runtime. That limitation is acceptable if it is explicit and the result establishes the path the product needs. The narrow slice should not fake the difficult boundary. If a demo skips readiness checks that the real consumer depends on, it has demonstrated presentation rather than the intended outcome. The aim is a small honest path, not a broad illusion. Write the result in terms a user can verify. “The acquisition subsystem is implemented” is weaker than “this consumer can use this selected resource after a normal acquisition and after the defined retry path.” The latter also reveals what remains outside the milestone. Distinguish blockers from ambitions A blocker prevents the selected result. An ambition improves or broadens a future result. They can both be important, but they should not occupy the same status. A missing runtime capability may block the chosen model. Support for every future provider probably does not. A resource-lifecycle defect may make the slice unsafe to release. A distributed scheduler may be unnecessary for a local-only first use. The distinction should be revisited when evidence changes. A supposedly optional feature may turn out to be required for the target user. A presumed dependency may disappear when an existing interface is understood. Keep the outcome visible so these revisions are possible. Price temporary choices honestly A narrow release often includes temporary decisions. They are not automatically technical debt, and they are not free. Record the condition under which they become costly. Supporting one runtime may be a sound product boundary. Hardcoding that runtime's private layout into every consumer may make the next integration unnecessarily expensive. A local implementation can be appropriate while still preserving a clear boundary where later variation is likely. The right question is not whether the design is future-proof. No design is. Ask whether it preserves the important current invariants and leaves a credible path for demonstrated next needs. Match qualification to the intended use Different projects may justify different balances. A personal tool can be useful with a narrow interface. A shared library needs clearer compatibility and failure contracts. A public service may require operational capabilities that a local prototype can defer. The development path should reflect those consequences. A receiving institution can also set conditions that the producer’s workflow cannot decide for it. Drew DeVault’s SourceHut account reports resource-use concerns while explicitly grounding its contribution restrictions primarily in ethical and political choices. It also acknowledges useful private AI review. The account should not be converted into a technical claim that the tools never work, or a controlled estimate that generated projects always cost more. It illustrates a practical boundary: a contributor’s preferred method does not determine another project’s admission rules. SourceHut policy account . Review the next user action For the work in hand, write the next useful action a person should be able to perform. Identify the one or two missing capabilities that actually prevent it. Then ask whether current foundational work removes those blockers. If it does, the connection should be easy to explain. If it does not, decide deliberately whether the research value justifies the delay. This is not a demand to abandon long-term work. It is a way to preserve agency over how much of the present is being spent on the future. The practical risk is not ambition itself. It is losing the line from today's work to a result someone can eventually use and evaluate.

title: 30 Make software understandable beyond source code
text: 30 Make software understandable beyond source code Source code describes executable structure, but it rarely contains the whole reason that structure exists. A developer can follow a call graph and still not know which requirement created a boundary, which alternative was rejected, or what evidence supports a claim of readiness. Connecting code representations with intent, decisions, applied guidance, and other information can help readers understand why software has its present structure. A visual representation should be evaluated through the questions it helps answer, rather than the fact that the result is a graph. Begin with a question that code alone answers poorly Consider: “If we change when a candidate becomes ready, which acceptance claims and consumers need review?” A call graph may identify callers. It may not identify a decision record explaining why the current boundary was chosen, or an acceptance observation made through a particular application. A useful representation could link the readiness decision to its contract, implementation owner, tests, consumers, and evidence. Each edge needs a meaning. “Related to” is too vague if readers use the graph to decide what must be checked. Another question is historical: “Why did we keep the old version available during preparation?” A source comment may explain it, or the reason may live in a discussion, plan, or failure report. The representation should help retrieve that reason without pretending every historical influence was recorded. Keep structural and semantic relationships distinct A code reference is an observed relationship in the implementation. A decision depends on a requirement is a semantic claim. A test supports an acceptance claim is an interpretation of what the test establishes. These edges have different evidence and maintenance needs. Automatically extracting references can populate one part of the graph. It cannot infer all intent relationships with equal authority. A generated edge may be a useful suggestion, but should remain attributable and revisable. RepoGraph reports benefits from code-relationship context for evaluated issue-resolution baselines. That is evidence about code retrieval in its setting. It does not validate a broader graph of intent, authority, and decisions. The broader design needs its own evaluation. RepoGraph . Design for reading rather than displaying everything A graph containing every node and edge can be less understandable than a short explanation. Readers need entry points, meaningful grouping, filtering, and progressive detail. For the readiness question, begin with the decision and immediate dependencies. Let the reader expand a consumer or inspect the supporting evidence. Do not force them to navigate the entire repository to answer a bounded question. Visual position and color should not carry unsupported meaning. A large node may look important even if its size merely reflects code references. A central position may suggest authority when it is only a layout artifact. Explain the encoding and provide a textual path through the same information. The representation also needs to show missing or stale evidence. An edge tied to an older revision may still be historically useful but should not silently certify the current implementation. Make the maintenance cost visible Every semantic relationship must come from somewhere. A person may record it, an agent may propose it, or a tool may derive it under explicit rules. Changes can invalidate it. If maintaining the graph takes more effort than the questions it answers justify, the system needs a narrower scope. Begin with a small set of valuable relationships rather than an ontology of all development knowledge. The graph may be a view over existing records rather than another source of truth. That can reduce duplication, provided the underlying records have stable meanings and identities. It also makes it possible to offer alternative views for different readers. Test comprehension directly Give a reader a concrete question and observe whether the representation helps them answer it correctly. Measure time if useful, but also inspect what they misunderstood. A fast wrong answer is not improved understanding. Compare the graph with a simpler baseline: a linked decision record, a searchable index, or a short narrative. The graph should earn its place through the relationship task, not through novelty. For an exercise, build a tiny map connecting one outcome, one design decision, one implementation boundary, and two pieces of evidence. Mark the provenance of every edge. Ask another developer what would need reconsideration if the outcome changed. Where the map suggests certainty it cannot support, revise the representation. The aim is software that can be understood and challenged beyond its source text. A visual model is one possible means to that end.

title: 31 Improve the development process itself
text: 31 Improve the development process itself A development method is also a system. It has users, interfaces, state, costs, and failure modes. It can accumulate compatibility layers, stale assumptions, and rituals that no longer serve their original purpose. If the method advocates proportionality, it must apply that principle to itself. A process can be too rigorous in the wrong way The inspected Planning Proportionality Recovery records describe a correction to an overgeneralized planning architecture. Generic transition and digest machinery had been applied too broadly. The repair restricted stale-state controls to work where independently prepared proposals could become outdated before integration. Multiple participants alone no longer implied that risk. A recorded read-only pilot prepared a temporary 132-line Pantograph plan and checked its structure and links while avoiding changes to a checkout with unrelated dirty documents. It did not implement the proposed product change. The case shows an accepted policy correction and bounded pilot, not a measured productivity improvement. Recovery plan ; pilot report . This is more instructive than a rule to always use a plan. The method recognized that a specialized safeguard was imposing obligations on tasks without the relevant hazard. It preserved scope, ownership, and acceptance while reducing unnecessary machinery. Identify the cost before adding a rule A new rule often follows a real failure. An agent used stale context, omitted a test, or changed a shared file without coordination. The natural response is to require another check everywhere. Before doing that, identify the conditions that made the failure possible. Does the risk apply to every task, or only to a particular concurrency pattern? Can the owner enforce it once instead of every caller documenting it? Is the new requirement likely to prevent the failure, or merely record that someone considered it? A safeguard can be valuable and still need a narrower trigger. It can also create new failure modes: blocked work, confusing authority, duplicated records, or false declarations of uncertainty. The Passeur proof-boundary case discussed in the coordination chapters illustrates why demanding more evidence is not automatically the correct contract. Distinguish compliance from effectiveness A workflow can be followed perfectly and produce a poor result. A developer can omit a prescribed artifact and still make a sound decision. Neither observation alone settles whether the workflow is useful. Compliance tells you whether the process occurred. Effectiveness asks whether it improved an outcome relative to a relevant alternative. The latter requires a comparison and careful attention to task differences. Choose a bounded improvement to investigate. Perhaps targeted guidance could replace a broad instruction dump. Perhaps a small serial task can omit a coordination record. Perhaps a runtime demonstration catches errors missed by the current tests. Define the outcome and the cost you will observe before changing the process. Boehm's risk-driven account treats both insufficient exploration and excessive exploration as risks, and scales effort and artifact detail to what a decision needs. It provides a useful conceptual basis for this work, without a universal formula for the optimal stopping point. Spiral Development Experience Principles and Refinements . Make criticism actionable Puma wants criticism to be one purpose of this book. The following questions are proposed prompts for that criticism, not invented statements about what Puma must believe: Where does the approach mistake a well-kept record for actual understanding? Which improvements may depend more on domain familiarity or model capability than on the method? Where would a direct implementation followed by user feedback be cheaper and equally dependable? Which important work is missing because it is difficult to represent or measure? Do the cases include enough rejected alternatives and adverse outcomes to judge the decisions? What can another developer reproduce, and what depends on individual judgment? A useful response identifies the claim being challenged and a condition or example that changes it. “This is too much process” becomes more actionable when it names the task class, the unnecessary obligation, and the simpler alternative. “This needs more rigor” becomes more useful when it identifies the failure the current evidence cannot exclude. Keep the method open without making every task a referendum Not every implementation should reopen the entire engineering philosophy. Stable guidance reduces repeated decision cost. The method needs a way to distinguish a local exception from evidence that a rule is wrong or mis-scoped. Record recurring friction. Look for patterns across tasks rather than treating one inconvenience as a universal defect. At the same time, do not require repeated harm before correcting a clear contradiction or dangerous boundary. The approach developed in this book is a set of relationships to preserve: purpose to behavior, concepts to invariants, authority to action, and claims to evidence. Its artifacts are means of preserving those relationships. Their form can change when a simpler or more effective method becomes available. That is the position readers are invited to examine. The work is not complete because the process has a name, the graph is connected, or the tests are green. It becomes useful when another person can understand what was intended, inspect what happened, judge what the evidence supports, and decide what to do next.

title: Working vocabulary
text: Working vocabulary These short definitions summarize how the book uses its terms. The linked chapters provide the examples and qualifications. They are aids to discussion, not a universal terminology standard. Acceptance. A decision that the stated outcome has been supported by the agreed evidence within a defined scope. It is distinct from finishing code, passing a test, or merging a branch. See chapter 27 . Agent interface. The operations, discovery paths, descriptions, feedback, and observable environment through which an agent uses a system. It includes errors and recovery, not only schemas. See chapter 12 . Authority. The right to make a decision or perform an action within a specified scope. Possessing information or a technical capability does not automatically grant it. See chapter 15 . Boundary. A set of promises separating responsibilities. A useful boundary exposes the distinctions callers need and contains incidental implementation choices. See chapter 9 . Candidate. In the running example, locally present material that has not yet met the conditions for publication as ready. See chapter 6 . Capability. A behavior a component can provide under stated conditions. A version label may be evidence about capability but is not identical to it. See chapter 9 . Characterization test. An experiment or test used to establish current behavior, often before changing unfamiliar code. It may reveal what exists without deciding whether that behavior is desirable. See chapter 3 . Contract. The obligations and permitted expectations between a component and its callers, including success, failure, identity, lifetime, and recovery where relevant. See chapter 9 . Decision record. A compact account of a consequential choice, its context, alternatives, status, and consequences. Its purpose is to preserve useful rationale rather than reproduce the entire discussion. See chapter 5 . Deterministic control. Enforcement whose result follows defined rules for the relevant input and state. It guarantees only the properties those rules actually check. See chapter 15 . Discovery. The conversational and investigative work of establishing what should be built and why, including uncertainty that may require a prototype or later revision. See chapter 2 . Domain model. A representation of concepts, identity, relationships, and rules needed to explain the problem's behavior. It need not map one-to-one to classes or services. See chapter 6 . Evidence boundary. The limit on what an observation supports: a revision, environment, path, population, or fault class, for example. See chapter 27 . Higher-order conflict. An incompatibility that can survive a clean text merge, such as disjoint changes violating the same semantic assumption or causing an integration failure. See chapter 20 . Hypothesis. A proposition being considered or tested, rather than an established fact or binding requirement. See chapter 2 . Identity. What allows a system to refer to the same thing across relevant changes. Resource identity, attempt identity, and artifact identity can have different lifetimes. See chapter 6 . Independent review. A procedure that gives a reviewer a separate opportunity to challenge a change. Separate roles do not guarantee statistically independent mistakes. See chapter 24 . Intent. The purpose and desired consequences motivating a request. It may require interpretation and can develop through investigation and use. See chapter 1 . Intent-oriented operation. An interface operation that requests a domain outcome while its owner handles incidental choreography, preserving consequential caller choices. See chapter 13 . Invariant. A condition that must remain true across the relevant states and transitions of a system. Its scope and owner must be clear. See chapter 7 . Lifecycle. The meaningful states and transitions of an activity or resource, including the obligations that remain after a caller stops waiting. See chapter 7 . Material uncertainty. An unresolved question that can change intended behavior, design, scope, or acceptance. It is not measured by patch size alone. See chapter 2 . Operational responsibility. The obligation to complete, clean up, or reconcile work. It can outlive the caller and differs from permission to initiate the work. See chapter 7 . Outcome. The behavior or capability that should become possible for the intended person or consumer. An implementation step is not necessarily an outcome. See chapter 1 . Proportionality. Matching investigation, abstraction, coordination, and evidence effort to the decisions and consequences at stake. It supports both adding and removing process. See chapter 31 . Provenance. Attributable relationships connecting artifacts, activities, actors, and sources. It helps reconstruction but does not by itself prove correctness, completeness, or causal explanation. See chapter 16 . Publication. In the running example, the transition that makes a candidate available through the consumer's agreed ready reference. It is distinct from completing transfer. See chapter 13 . Readiness. The bounded promise that the resource satisfies the conditions required for the intended next use. Its meaning must be defined by the contract. See chapter 7 . Refactoring. A change intended to improve internal structure while preserving required behavior. In practice, mixed changes require care when attributing benefits or defects. See chapter 10 . Revision guard. A check that a proposal applies to the state or version against which it was prepared. Passing it does not prove the proposal serves the intended outcome. See chapter 15 . Running example. The explicitly illustrative resource-acquisition system developed through this book. It is not a reconstruction of any one implementation. See chapter 1 . Shared foundation. A layer whose responsibility serves demonstrated common needs across consumers, while preserving application-specific meaning where appropriate. See chapter 28 . Test oracle. The basis used to judge whether an observed result is correct. An oracle can encode the same mistaken assumption as the implementation. See chapter 23 . Uncertain outcome. A situation in which the observer cannot yet establish whether an operation's side effect occurred. It requires reconciliation or defined retry semantics, not an invented success or failure. See chapter 25 . Vertical slice. An end-to-end increment that lets a person or consumer achieve a bounded useful result through the necessary layers. See chapter 29 .
